items: [A | guideline supported] A Korean joint guideline using a GRADE-based systematic review found that early RAS blockade delays progression to kidney failure and improves long-term survival. The greatest benefit was seen when started at the microscopic hematuria or microalbuminuria stage. The guideline makes no recommendation for routine use of cyclosporine, MRAs or SGLT2 inhibitors. - PMID:42316418

[A | guideline supported] Guidelines advise caution with living-related donation from relatives carrying COL4A variants. The 2024 guideline says heterozygous relatives should be considered only as a last resort. The 2013 guideline discourages affected mothers of X-linked males from donating because of their own risk of kidney failure. - PMID:23349312, PMID:39673454

[A | guideline supported] KDIGO 2026 recommends individualised Hb thresholds for ESA initiation. It sets an upper Hb target below 11.5 g/dL during ESA maintenance therapy. - PMID:41485807, PMID:42735412

[A | guideline supported] KDIGO 2026 requires correctable causes of anaemia to be addressed before an ESA or HIF-PHI is used. It recommends an ESA rather than a HIF-PHI as first-line treatment, once alternative causes are excluded and iron deficiency is corrected. - PMID:42095795, PMID:42414122, PMID:42735412

[B | guideline supported] The ERKNet/ERA/ESPN 2024 guideline recommends that relatives carrying heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 variants be considered for living kidney donation only as a last resort. This is relevant because potential living donors in this maternal-line X-linked family may be heterozygous carriers. - PMID:39673454

[B | established] A 2024 international guideline (ERKNet/ERA/ESPN), based on a systematic review of PICO questions, states that early RAS blockade is the standard of care for COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy, including Alport syndrome. It adds that SGLT2 inhibitors may be added in adults with proteinuria and CKD. (verified with caveat) - PMID:39673454

[B | guideline supported] KDIGO 2026 uses TSAT and ferritin thresholds to guide iron therapy. It prefers IV over oral iron in haemodialysis, with a proactive IV approach. Broader initiation thresholds are proposed in non-dialysis CKD, and iron should be withheld during systemic infection. The numeric TSAT and ferritin cut-offs are not given in the provided sources. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42414122, PMID:42735412

[B | guideline supported] Guidelines universally use serum ferritin to define iron deficiency, and about half add TSAT. Across conditions, the systematic review of guidelines concludes that a ferritin cut-off of 100 μg/L and a TSAT of 20% should be considered in most conditions. - PMID:26561626

[B | guideline supported] For iron treatment monitoring, guidelines proposed ferritin targets above 100 μg/L or 200 μg/L. In CKD, some recommended that ferritin should not exceed 500 μg/L or 800 μg/L. Only 9 guidelines set TSAT targets, ranging from 20% to 50%. - PMID:26561626

[B | guideline supported] On route of iron: reviews report that IV iron is preferred in dialysis-dependent CKD (5D), and either IV or oral iron is recommended in non-dialysis CKD stages 3-5. CKD is listed among indications for IV iron. - PMID:26561626, PMID:30970355, PMID:40159291

[B | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of CKD patients, each 1% increase in RDW was associated with a 47% higher risk of all-cause mortality. In the haemodialysis subgroup the increase was 36%. - PMID:28916240

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review supporting the KDOQI 2015 hemodialysis adequacy update found moderate-quality evidence that earlier dialysis initiation did not reduce mortality compared with later initiation. - PMID:26498415

[B | guideline supported] The ERKNet/ERA/ESPN guideline advises that relatives carrying heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 variants be considered only as the last possible resource for living kidney donation. - PMID:39673454

[B | guideline supported] Early RAS blockade delays progression to kidney failure and improves long-term survival in Alport syndrome. The benefit is greatest when started at the microscopic hematuria or microalbuminuria stage. The guideline does not report benefit data for initiation or continuation at CKD G4-G5. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42316418

[C | evidence supported] KDIGO eGFR categories define G5 as eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 in people not on kidney replacement therapy. The patient's latest CKD-EPI 2021 eGFR of 6.2 mL/min/1.73 m2 falls in this category. - PMID:34571286

[C | emerging] A rapid fall in eGFR in someone with established CKD fits the reviewed concept of acute-on-chronic kidney disease. That review reports creatinine-based definitions are less accurate prognostically in CKD, while cystatin C-based eGFR discriminates mortality and progression better. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] In a CKD cohort, a large positive difference between creatinine-based and cystatin C-based eGFR was associated with higher MACE risk and faster coronary artery calcification progression. This is an association, not proof of causation. - PMID:34571286

[C | evidence supported] Drug-dosing thresholds based on Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance are not interchangeable with CKD-EPI eGFR. The discordance leads to discordant doses in 4-34% of patients depending on the agent, with the largest gaps at the lowest measured function. - PMID:42939623

[C | evidence supported] For people at high risk of CKD, eGFR, urine albumin-creatinine ratio and blood pressure should be measured regularly. In real-world data, cardiovascular and renal risk rises as eGFR declines and albuminuria worsens. - PMID:39162984, PMID:41173585

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalemia is defined as serum potassium greater than 5.0 mEq/L and hypokalemia as less than 3.5 mEq/L. The patient's latest K of 5.2 mmol/L exceeds this hyperkalemia threshold (mild range). - PMID:36689973

[C | evidence supported] Emergent hyperkalemia treatment is recommended for clinical signs or symptoms (e.g., muscle weakness, paralysis) or ECG abnormalities. ECG may not correlate with serum potassium. Dialysis may be considered in end-stage renal disease or severe renal impairment. - PMID:36689973

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalemia prevalence rises steeply as eGFR falls, reaching 47.5% in CKD G5, with severe hyperkalemia in 10.5% of G5 patients. Sample-processing factors (pseudohyperkalemia) were independently associated with elevated results, so sample processing should be optimised. - PMID:42122012

[C | evidence supported] Guidelines (KDIGO 2024, as summarised in reviews) advise individualised potassium management. This means adjusting dietary potassium to keep serum K in the normal range and limiting foods rich in bioavailable potassium, especially processed foods, rather than reflexively restricting fruits and vegetables. Hyperkalemia risk is modified by kidney function, bowel function, metabolic acidosis, glycaemia and medications. - PMID:32872726, PMID:42650632

[C | evidence supported] A review-proposed, evidence-aligned monitoring and management strategy includes correcting constipation and acidosis, reviewing potassium-raising medications and additives, and monitoring serum potassium according to baseline risk. - PMID:42650632

[C | evidence supported] Patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate are recommended by international guidelines for hyperkalemia management. A US consensus addresses K monitoring before and during binder use, binder use with RAAS inhibitors and dialysis, and timing and duration of binder use. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is associated with serious GI adverse effects. - PMID:36689973, PMID:39577885

[C | evidence supported] In hypertensive CKD, most patients (especially with albuminuria) should receive a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor. Hyperkalemia should be managed with low-potassium dietary advice and oral binders to avoid stopping prognostically beneficial medications. - PMID:42035931

[C | evidence supported] Anaemia is described as a common complication of CKD, often treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs). The source states that the optimal Hb target remains uncertain. - PMID:42893801

[C | emerging] In an emulated target trial of haemodialysis patients under protocolised darbepoetin dosing, an Hb target of 105-125 g/L was not associated with increased 8-month all-cause mortality compared with 95-115 g/L. - PMID:42893801

[C | emerging] Targeting Hb above 125 g/L (125-145 vs 95-115 g/L) may increase mortality risk, though the estimate was imprecise. The authors note this is consistent with previous trial findings. - PMID:42893801

[C | evidence supported] CKD patients have a suboptimal response to vaccines, including hepatitis B vaccine. One narrative review suggests testing anti-HBs after vaccination and giving booster doses when titres fall below the seroprotective level (<10 IU/mL). - PMID:33423842, PMID:36165374

[C | emerging] In data cited by the review, hepatitis B vaccine seroprotection with an adjuvanted vaccine was higher in pre-dialysis than in dialysis patients (95% vs 82%). This indirectly suggests that vaccinating before dialysis may give better responses. - PMID:33423842

[C | evidence supported] Infection is the second most common cause of death in CKD after cardiovascular disease, and vaccination is described as an important part of care in kidney disease, including dialysis and transplant. - PMID:30876620

[C | evidence supported] An Indian expert consensus defines adults aged 18-59 with comorbidities as a target group. It recommends Tdap every 10 years, annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV13/PPSV23 series), hepatitis B and meningococcal vaccines, and risk-based hepatitis A. Zoster is listed for those aged 50 and over. - PMID:42388548
[C | evidence supported] A JAMA review reports that sexually active people aged 15-44 should be screened for syphilis at least once, and at least annually if at increased risk. - PMID:41100079

[C | evidence supported] Australia's national hepatitis B strategy calls for population-wide testing to establish hepatitis B status, because risk-based testing is considered insufficient. Chronic hepatitis B is often asymptomatic. - PMID:42935728

[C | evidence supported] In transplantation from HBV-positive donors, recipient management depends on recipient HBV immunity. Antiviral prophylaxis may be considered in susceptible non-liver (e.g., kidney) recipients but is not recommended in immune non-liver recipients. - PMID:25707744

[C | evidence supported] The USPSTF gives a Grade D recommendation against screening asymptomatic males for testicular cancer, by either self-examination or clinical examination. Authors of an advocacy review dispute this and request a Grade B. - PMID:29717912

[C | evidence supported] Hearing loss and ocular lesions are core extrarenal features of Alport syndrome. The sources therefore support baseline hearing and eye assessment in a male with suspected X-linked disease. - PMID:12105244, PMID:17570934, PMID:39384344

[C | emerging] Deafness and lenticonus are consistent within families for a given COL4A5 mutation. Knowing the genotype adds prognostic information on extrarenal disease. Non-glycine or 3' glycine missense variants were associated with fewer extrarenal symptoms. - PMID:12105244
[C | emerging] In a retrospective Chinese adult Alport cohort, eye and ear impairment was associated with higher risk of kidney failure or CKD stage 3b. - PMID:41767691

[C | evidence supported] De novo anti-GBM disease after kidney transplantation for Alport syndrome is described as a recognised phenomenon. It is a consideration for post-transplant planning and monitoring. - PMID:28515156

[C | evidence supported] Molecular diagnosis can support safer assessment of living-related donors. However, a variant of uncertain significance should not by itself determine treatment or donor eligibility, and segregation and phenotype should be weighed. - PMID:42792963

[C | evidence supported] In a real-world cohort with measured GFR (iohexol clearance), the combined creatinine-cystatin C equation (eGFRcr-cys) was more accurate than either creatinine or cystatin C alone when the two estimates were highly discordant. When they agreed, all three equations performed similarly. When cystatin C eGFR was lower than creatinine eGFR, creatinine eGFR overestimated measured GFR and cystatin C eGFR underestimated it. - PMID:36995139

[C | evidence supported] In over 400,000 UK Biobank participants, reassigning CKD stage using cystatin C instead of creatinine moved 15% to a more advanced stage. Reclassification became more frequent as the number of long-term conditions rose. The authors suggest considering cystatin C alongside creatinine to refine kidney function estimation and risk stratification. - PMID:42858001

[C | evidence supported] A primary-care review states that, when possible, serum cystatin C should be measured to confirm eGFR in patients with CKD. The measured-GFR study similarly notes that cystatin C is recommended as a confirmatory test when more precise estimates are needed for clinical decisions. - PMID:36995139, PMID:38215416

[C | emerging] A critical review of acute-on-chronic kidney disease reports that creatinine-based definitions have reduced prognostic accuracy in CKD populations. By contrast, cystatin C-based eGFR shows better discrimination for mortality and CKD progression. - PMID:42954720
[C | emerging] Point-of-care cystatin C systems remain investigational. Results near major clinical decision thresholds should be confirmed. - PMID:42783394

[C | evidence supported] A 2013 expert guideline (Level D / Level III evidence) recommends RAS blockade for males with X-linked Alport syndrome, possibly even before proteinuria onset. It also recommends identifying and following all affected family members, including most mothers of affected males. - PMID:23349312

[C | evidence supported] The Korean guideline reports that cyclosporine and MRAs lowered proteinuria in the short term without sustained renoprotection. Cyclosporine carries a substantial risk of nephrotoxicity, and evidence for SGLT2 inhibitors is inconsistent in Alport syndrome. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42316418

[C | emerging] For monitoring, a narrative review states that, in children, no podocyte-derived urinary marker has been shown to add information beyond proteinuria and filtration rate. The provided sources give no Alport-specific monitoring interval for eGFR or albuminuria. - PMID:42942308

[C | evidence supported] Genetic testing is described as the gold standard for diagnosing Alport syndrome and establishing its mode of inheritance. A narrative review cautions that variants of uncertain significance should not on their own determine treatment or donor eligibility, and should be evaluated against segregation and phenotype. - PMID:23349312, PMID:42792963

[C | evidence supported] A 2026 review reports that KDIGO guidance on metabolic acidosis in CKD consists of practice points, not graded recommendations. These practice points suggest considering treatment to prevent metabolic acidosis at a proposed serum bicarbonate cutoff of <18 mmol/L. The review's authors argue this cutoff leaves many people with CKD untreated and call for the practice points to be revised. - PMID:42349771

[C | evidence supported] Earlier guidelines, including KDOQI, recommended alkali therapy targeting serum bicarbonate ≥22 mEq/L. This was based mainly on nutrition and bone concerns, and later guidelines suggested similar targets for possibly slowing CKD progression. Adequately powered long-term RCTs on efficacy and safety are described as largely lacking, and practice varies. - PMID:36175070, PMID:36916426

[C | evidence supported] Metabolic acidosis affects about 30% of patients with advanced CKD. In CKD it is associated with hyperkalemia, more rapid CKD progression, muscle wasting, bone disease and mortality. These are associations, not proven causal effects. - PMID:36175070, PMID:36916426

[C | evidence supported] Metabolic acidosis is listed as one modifier of hyperkalemia risk in CKD, alongside kidney function, bowel function, diabetes, medications and food factors. Correcting metabolic acidosis, for example with sodium bicarbonate, is described as one approach to managing hyperkalemia. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, a potassium binder, raised serum bicarbonate in potassium-endpoint trials. - PMID:36916426, PMID:42196253, PMID:42650632

[C | emerging] Evidence that alkali therapy (mainly sodium bicarbonate) preserves kidney function or improves patient outcomes in CKD is conflicting. Well-powered trials of efficacy and safety are still needed. An older review states that base therapy for chronic metabolic acidosis is associated with improved cellular function and few complications. - PMID:20308999, PMID:38791238

[C | evidence supported] The first step in working up metabolic acidosis is determining whether an anion gap is present. This requires serum sodium, chloride and bicarbonate. Osmolal gap, urine pH and serum potassium may help in certain settings. - PMID:40175031

[C | emerging] For patients on chronic hemodialysis, one 2003 review recommends measuring post-dialysis blood bicarbonate at least monthly, with a management goal of serum bicarbonate ≥22 mmol/L. This is the only explicit acid-base monitoring interval in the provided sources, and it applies only once maintenance hemodialysis is established. - PMID:12649614

[C | emerging] An emergency-medicine narrative review states that IV calcium is primarily indicated when there are ECG changes or serum potassium is ≥6.5 mmol/L. This is an acute-management threshold, not a chronic target for CKD G5 or dialysis initiation. - PMID:41506858
[C | evidence supported] Haemodialysis is described as the definitive option for refractory hyperkalaemia or for hyperkalaemia in end-stage renal disease. - PMID:41506858

[C | emerging] In non-dialysis CKD, hyperkalaemia is defined as serum K >5.0 mmol/L and normokalaemia as 3.5-5.0 mmol/L. A KDIGO-2024-based quality-improvement protocol monitors potassium every 3 months, or monthly in high-risk patients. - PMID:42015032

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalaemia above 6 mmol/L is very common in patients on chronic haemodialysis: about 41-42% in both arms of the ALCHEMIST RCT over a median follow-up of 32.6 months. - PMID:40818851

[C | evidence supported] Evidence supports acute potassium shifting with insulin plus glucose, salbutamol, or both, which lower K on average by 0.7-1.2 mmol/L (very low to low certainty). Insulin-glucose carries a considerable risk of hypoglycaemia, particularly in non-diabetic patients with low baseline glucose. - PMID:39761907, PMID:41506858

[C | evidence supported] The Spanish Society of Nephrology adaptation of KDIGO 2026 describes individualised ESA initiation at Hb 8.5–10 g/dL. This depends on cardiovascular risk, symptoms and transfusion needs, with a threshold of ≥9–10 g/dL in dialysis. It retains an Hb target below 11.5 g/dL. - PMID:42414122

[C | evidence supported] Experts note that robust evidence on optimal thresholds for starting iron and on target iron parameters remains lacking. They also note US ferritin targets in haemodialysis are higher than elsewhere. - PMID:42095795, PMID:42670634

[C | evidence supported] The only monitoring or titration cadence stated in the sources is ESA or HIF-PHI dose adjustment every 4 weeks, using the lowest effective dose. No source specifies a guideline Hb or iron-index monitoring frequency for CKD G5, with or without dialysis. - PMID:42414122

[C | evidence supported] Use of HIF-PHIs is restricted, and they have safety signals. The SEN adaptation reserves them for non-dialysis CKD when ESAs are unsuitable, and in the US the single approved product is limited to patients on dialysis for at least 3 months. A meta-analysis found reduced transfusion with no significant MACE or mortality increase, but a hyperkalaemia signal in non-dialysis patients. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42095795, PMID:42414122, PMID:42819330
[C | evidence supported] Patient Blood Management strategies to reduce transfusion are promoted, particularly in kidney transplant candidates. - PMID:42414122

[C | evidence supported] Intravenous iron agents carry a reported risk of hypophosphataemia and 6H syndrome. KDOQI highlights the incidence and significance of hypophosphataemia in non-dialysis CKD patients receiving IV iron. - PMID:34758368, PMID:42095795

[C | evidence supported] CKD-specific criteria (per a review summarising guidelines) define absolute iron deficiency as TSAT ≤20% plus ferritin ≤100 ng/mL in predialysis or peritoneal dialysis patients, or ≤200 ng/mL on haemodialysis. Functional iron deficiency (iron-restricted erythropoiesis) is defined as TSAT ≤20% with elevated ferritin. The review states that all CKD patients should be screened for anaemia. - PMID:30970355

[C | evidence supported] An alternative CKD definition, adopted about 25 years ago, counts iron deficiency as ferritin <100 μg/L regardless of TSAT, or ferritin 100-299 μg/L if TSAT is <20%. The authors note that this threshold was set to encourage iron use alongside ESAs rather than being validated against tissue iron depletion. - PMID:38733252

[C | evidence supported] Ferritin is distorted by inflammation, which is common in CKD. The general-population ferritin cut-off (typically <30 ng/mL) applies to people without inflammatory conditions, so higher CKD-specific thresholds are used. - PMID:38733252, PMID:40159291

[C | emerging] The percentage of hypochromic red cells (%HYPO) and reticulocyte haemoglobin content (CHr) are described as the most specific markers of iron-deficient erythropoiesis in non-dialysis CKD, but their availability is limited. - PMID:28963827

[C | emerging] Ferritin interpretation can be altered by SGLT2 inhibitors (and possibly neprilysin inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists). Medication use should therefore be documented when reading iron studies. - PMID:38733252, PMID:42559859

[C | evidence supported] Newer IV iron preparations carry a reported risk of hypophosphataemia and 6H syndrome, which includes hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. This is a relevant safety consideration in advanced CKD. - PMID:34758368

[C | emerging] In a large non-dialysis CKD cohort, RDW was the only CBC-derived marker that remained independently associated with all-cause mortality after multivariable adjustment. NLR added prognostic information only when RDW was not elevated. - PMID:42329902

[C | emerging] In hospitalised adults with advanced non-dialysis CKD in an Indian tertiary centre, RDW independently predicted in-hospital mortality, but its discrimination alone was only moderate. - PMID:42255783

[C | evidence supported] RDW is traditionally used in the differential diagnosis of anaemia and has broad, nonspecific prognostic value. It is not established whether elevated RDW is causal or an epiphenomenon of inflammation, poor nutrition, oxidative stress or altered erythropoietin function. - PMID:25535770

[C | emerging] The RDW-to-albumin ratio (RAR) was independently associated with all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality in a US CKD cohort. It also predicted poor outcomes in dialysis patients with coronary artery disease. - PMID:42110186, PMID:42789467

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews recommend obtaining optimal vaccination status before solid organ transplantation whenever possible. The stated reasons are that vaccine responses are reduced after transplant (especially early post-transplant or after rejection treatment) and that some vaccines are contraindicated post-transplant. - PMID:37897013, PMID:38043106, PMID:39588050

[C | evidence supported] In a single-center cohort of adult kidney transplant candidates, prior vaccination and seropositivity rates were low. Only 5% had complete immunization or seropositivity. Seropositivity for hepatitis B surface antibody was 66%, hepatitis A IgG 30%, and measles 88%, mumps 78%, rubella 90% and varicella 96%. Vaccine uptake was high once candidates were offered vaccination, although hepatitis A vaccine was declined relatively often. - PMID:37781169

[C | emerging] In a pediatric transplant cohort, a proportion of fully vaccinated patients were seronegative for varicella (23.6%) and measles (13.0%). Vaccination status also changed between evaluation and transplant. This indirectly supports checking serologic immunity to live-vaccine-preventable infections during the pre-transplant window. - PMID:38043106, PMID:42591271

[C | evidence supported] A review of non-HIV immunosuppressed women reports increased HPV, squamous intraepithelial lesion and cervical cancer risk in ESRD and SOT recipients. It recommends a 3-dose HPV vaccine series for age-eligible patients, with catch-up to age 26, initiated and completed before SOT when possible. - PMID:39804372

[C | emerging] In heart transplant candidates on ventricular assist devices, an inactivated hepatitis A vaccine series produced seroconversion in all 35 participants, with only minor adverse events. The authors recommend completing hepatitis A vaccination before transplantation if indicated. - PMID:42565867
[C | emerging] Structured post-transplant vaccine reviews were associated with increased vaccine coverage (including PPV23 and HPV) in pediatric SOT recipients. - PMID:42957987
[C | evidence supported] No CMV vaccine has achieved regulatory approval, so CMV prevention in transplant recipients currently relies on other strategies. - PMID:42800022

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review states that pre-transplant HPV vaccination is ideal for age-eligible kidney transplant recipients. It also notes that these patients carry a disproportionate HPV-related disease burden because of prolonged immunosuppression. - PMID:27772624

[C | evidence supported] Kidney transplant recipients face elevated risk of persistent high-risk HPV infection and anal squamous cell carcinoma, attributed to immunosuppression impairing immunosurveillance. HPV also causes penile and head and neck cancers, which are relevant to males. - PMID:27772624, PMID:42654785

[C | emerging] In non-dialysis CKD, a meta-analysis reported 100% seroconversion after HPV vaccination, but with lower neutralising antibody levels. The authors caution that surrogate markers may not reflect clinical effectiveness. - PMID:42079457

[C | emerging] A systematic review of non-HIV immunocompromised individuals (including solid organ transplant recipients) found HPV vaccination immunogenic and safe, with rare serious adverse events judged unrelated to vaccination. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. The only effectiveness data (cervical lesions) showed rate ratios near the null. - PMID:42011219

[C | evidence supported] General CKD/transplant vaccination reviews state that vaccinations are generally safe in CKD and should follow public health recommendations. They note that immunosuppression after transplant further impairs vaccine responses, which supports vaccinating before transplant. Vaccination is also listed as a primary cancer-prevention strategy after kidney transplant. - PMID:41597712, PMID:41759616, PMID:41958670
[C | evidence supported] Vaccination coverage in CKD patients is reported as suboptimal. In one single-centre cohort, HPV vaccination coverage among hemodialysis patients was 0%. - PMID:42646674

[C | evidence supported] Reviews of the IDEAL randomized trial report no significant difference in survival or patient-centred outcomes between early and late initiation. They note the trial challenged eGFR as the primary guide and supports the safety of waiting for symptoms or lower eGFR. - PMID:22388556, PMID:28410652
[C | evidence supported] The transition from CKD stage 5 through the first year of dialysis is a period of exceptionally high vulnerability, with annual mortality above 20%. - PMID:28410652

[C | emerging] Starting conventional in-centre haemodialysis is associated with higher initial mortality, especially with temporary catheters, and PD starters appear to have better initial outcomes. One review also notes that creatinine-based eGFR may misclassify patients with muscle wasting or fluid overload. - PMID:25556306

[C | emerging] In a retrospective cohort, pre-dialysis coordinator review at CKD stage 5 and referral within 90 days of initiation were associated with more unplanned dialysis starts (starts without permanent access). Review at eGFR 9-14 was associated with lower risk. - PMID:42870239

[C | evidence supported] Post-transplant anti-GBM disease is reported to affect up to approximately 5% of Alport syndrome transplant recipients. The figure applies to all Alport genotypes combined; no X-linked-specific rate is given. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[C | evidence supported] Absence of the α3α4α5(IV) network in the Alport GBM is thought to cause loss of immunologic tolerance to the donor GBM. In X-linked disease the alloantigen most often implicated is α5(IV). An earlier report found α3(IV) to be the target in an X-linked patient with complete COL4A5 deletion. - PMID:12778332, PMID:42390934, PMID:7783419

[C | evidence supported] When post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis occurs it is severe and usually leads to graft loss. Onset is typically within weeks to months and usually not beyond the first year. It recurs and progresses rapidly after retransplantation in multiple reported patients. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[C | evidence supported] Selection criteria described for carrier donors: donation is generally avoided, but may be considered in highly selected individuals older than 40 years with preserved kidney function and no subclinical kidney damage on kidney biopsy. Evaluation should be careful and individualized. - PMID:42147990

[C | emerging] Whole-exome sequencing of living donors found that 13.1% carried variants linked to latent renal or systemic conditions despite no clinical signs at donation. This indirectly supports genetic screening of related donor candidates. - PMID:41194031

[C | emerging] The sources contain no data on cystatin C or combined equation accuracy specifically at eGFR <15 or near kidney failure. The broadest comparison (>70 studies in CKD, transplant, T2D and PKD) found eGFR frequently deviated from mGFR by ±30% or more and misstaged CKD in 30-60% of patients. Errors were comparable whether equations used creatinine, cystatin C, or both. - PMID:30518813

[C | emerging] A recent review states that the 2024 KDIGO guideline recommends combined creatinine-cystatin C equations for CKD diagnosis and staging. It also states that cystatin C-inclusive equations generally outperform creatinine-only equations in bias and accuracy, including in patients with comorbidities. Another review suggests eGFRcys or eGFRcr-cys as confirmatory tests when creatinine is less precise or a more valid estimate is needed for decisions. Neither source reports performance at eGFR <15. - PMID:39125705, PMID:42424121

[C | emerging] In 50 nephrotic patients with membranous nephropathy, combined equations performed acceptably only without hypoalbuminemia. Biases increased as hypoalbuminemia worsened. The authors conclude that direct GFR measurement is needed for individual clinical decisions, including dosing of renally cleared toxic drugs. - PMID:42761225

[C | emerging] In ADPKD, combining creatinine and cystatin C improved precision and reduced variability of eGFR slope against measured GFR. This is indirect evidence that combined estimates may track rapid decline more reliably than creatinine alone. - PMID:42733501

[C | emerging] Cystatin C levels can be affected by non-renal factors, notably steroid therapy. In pooled CKD-EPI data, 20-70% of eGFR-mGFR deviations came from patient-level error in eGFR, so individual estimates carry substantial uncertainty. - PMID:11928770, PMID:42804441

[C | emerging] In a large population cohort (UK Biobank), creatinine- and cystatin C-based eGFR (EKFC equations) were frequently discordant. Re-staging with eGFRcys moved 15% of participants to a more advanced CKD stage. Discordance was associated with demographic factors and long-term conditions, and increased with multimorbidity. The authors suggest considering cystatin C alongside creatinine in multimorbid individuals. Age-specific (young adult) or hereditary glomerular disease subgroups are not reported in the abstract. - PMID:42858001

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews note that serum cystatin C has non-renal determinants. Steroid therapy is named specifically, the influence of malignancy is uncertain, and an epidemiological association with mildly raised CRP is described. These could bias cystatin C-based eGFR independently of filtration. – of these factors was evaluated in Alport syndrome or young adults. - PMID:11928770, PMID:16838182

[C | evidence supported] Reviews describe serum cystatin C as an endogenous GFR marker, with probable superiority over creatinine as a screening test for early renal dysfunction. They also note a lack of prospective studies confirming its prognostic significance. The sources do not address its performance in advanced CKD (G5). - PMID:11040958, PMID:11928770

[C | evidence supported] Serum creatinine lags behind an acute fall in kidney function. Immediately after a renal insult, creatinine may still be in the normal range, and a fall in urine output may be the only sign. A single creatinine-based estimate taken during rapid change may therefore not reflect current GFR. - PMID:28722925

[C | evidence supported] A source summarising the 2026 KDIGO AKI criteria reports two things. First, a suggestion (2B) to use serum cystatin C to identify AKI when serum creatinine is less accurate. Second, a practice point that a baseline serum creatinine should be ascertained for all patients with suspected or confirmed AKI. - PMID:28722925

[C | emerging] Serum creatinine-based equations perform reasonably at population level but show substantial individual-level imprecision and inaccuracy. One perspective proposes exogenous measured GFR (iohexol) for individualised decisions. - PMID:42274272

[C | evidence supported] Renal dose-adjustment guidance is reported as well established for stable CKD but less certain in AKI, where renal function can change rapidly. In an ICU cohort, 51% of patient-medication pairs were discordant with reference renal-dosing recommendations. - PMID:42903729
[C | emerging] Results near major clinical decision thresholds should be confirmed, and assay-specific validation and calibration traceability matter for kidney function testing. - PMID:42783394

[C | evidence supported] Kidney transplantation is described as usually very successful in Alport syndrome, with excellent long-term outcomes. Donor eligibility, genotype-specific prognosis and post-transplant complications remain clinical considerations. - PMID:10499074, PMID:42076904

[C | evidence supported] Post-transplant anti-GBM disease is reported in up to about 5% of Alport patients. COL4A5 defects account for most cases, and α5(IV)NC1 is the usual alloantibody target. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[C | evidence supported] Mechanistically, the intact donor α3α4α5(IV) network is a non-tolerised antigen. In X-linked Alport patients the alloantigen most often implicated is α5(IV), whereas in autosomal recessive disease it is α3(IV). - PMID:42390934

[C | evidence supported] When post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis occurs, graft failure typically happens within weeks to months and usually within the first year. Progression to graft loss is often rapid and nearly always ends in graft loss. An isolated serological form (antibodies without clinical nephritis) also exists. - PMID:10499074, PMID:42390934

[C | emerging] There is no agreed protocol for prophylaxis or treatment of post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis in Alport syndrome. Reported strategies vary and include steroid-based immunosuppression combinations and plasmapheresis. - PMID:42390934

[C | emerging] In a regional paediatric cohort tested for COL4A3/COL4A4/COL4A5 with ACMG classification, glycine-substituting missense variants were the most frequent molecular defect (9/18). Cascade testing found additional genetically affected relatives in every family tested. - PMID:42552945

[C | evidence supported] Expert guidance advocates genetic testing for persistent hematuria and cascade testing of first-degree relatives. It recommends that COL4A3/COL4A4 heterozygotes not act as kidney donors, and that in digenic Alport syndrome affected family members be identified, treated, and discouraged from kidney donation. - PMID:34930753, PMID:35675912

[C | evidence supported] Disease severity in the Alport spectrum is described as varying with variant type, allelic dosage, sex, and genetic modifiers. A hemizygous male with a pathogenic COL4A5 variant has all α3α4α5(IV) heterotrimers affected. - PMID:35675912, PMID:42614610

[C | evidence supported] Clinical practice recommendations advise starting ACE inhibition at the time of diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome. This framing is about early disease, not advanced CKD. - PMID:33159213

[C | emerging] In a retrospective multicentre cohort of Indian children with COL4A variants, many with CKD, ACEI/ARB use showed no significant impact on proteinuria or CKD at 5-year follow-up. - PMID:42955332

[C | hypothesis] Mechanistic review: proteinuria from podocyte foot-process effacement may be partly modifiable, whereas proteinuria from podocyte loss and glomerulosclerosis (later disease) is less likely to be reversible. This suggests, without testing it, that antiproteinuric therapy may yield less benefit at late stages. - PMID:42949772

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalemia is identified as an important safety consideration needing serum potassium monitoring when nonsteroidal MRAs are used, including with SGLT2i. These data come from non-Alport populations. No source quantifies hyperkalemia risk for ACEi/ARB or SGLT2i at CKD G4-G5. - PMID:42171960, PMID:42469710

[C | emerging] In a prospective CKD cohort (KNOW-CKD), a persistently low serum total CO2 trajectory was associated with a higher risk of renal events than an intermediate trajectory. This is an observational association and does not establish causation. - PMID:42529231

[C | emerging] A meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found that veverimer, described as an experimental oral acid-binding polymer, increased serum bicarbonate versus placebo. Adverse events were not significantly different between groups. The outcome is a surrogate, not a patient-important outcome. - PMID:41723402

[C | emerging] For patients on maintenance haemodialysis, a narrative review reports no consensus on the optimal frequency of routine laboratory testing. Recommendations vary across guidelines and robust evidence is limited. - PMID:41484839

[C | emerging] A narrative review notes that metabolic acidosis is one of the factors modifying hyperkalaemia risk in CKD. It recommends correcting acidosis as part of an individualised potassium strategy. - PMID:42650632

[D | hypothesis] In non-dialysis CKD G3-G5, sarcopenia was associated with lower serum creatinine. Reduced muscle mass may therefore lower creatinine and make creatinine-based kidney function estimates less reliable. - PMID:35463026

[D | emerging] Potassium-enriched salt substitutes lack clinical guidelines for routine use, and clinicians report concerns about safety risks. Dietary review in advanced CKD should therefore ask about salt-substitute use. - PMID:42877676

[D | hypothesis] Extrarenal features help discriminate between Alport inheritance forms. Typical hearing loss and ocular abnormalities are absent in autosomal dominant Alport syndrome. However, a male with a COL4A5 glycine missense variant may present without extrarenal manifestations, so their absence does not exclude X-linked disease. - PMID:33748275, PMID:42172079

[D | emerging] A three-patient case series reports kidney transplantation as effective in genetically confirmed Alport syndrome, including X-linked cases, when guided by molecular confirmation and careful donor evaluation. Late antibody-mediated rejection and vascular events occurred, underscoring the need for individualised surveillance. - PMID:42076904

[D | emerging] Hyperkalaemia after the long interdialytic interval is described as potentially life-threatening. One single-arm study screened for it using pre-dialysis K >5.3 mmol/L and tracked pre-dialysis potassium at weeks 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24 and 52. - PMID:42572755

[D | hypothesis] In maintenance haemodialysis patients, higher RDW was independently associated with late arteriovenous fistula thrombosis. A cutoff of ≥15.30% had high specificity but low sensitivity. - PMID:41909600

[D | hypothesis] A single case report describes new HLA class I donor-specific antibodies and a positive flow crossmatch after PCV13 and recombinant zoster vaccination in a kidney waitlisted patient with a planned live donor. The authors suggest that these vaccines or their adjuvants can potentially cause allosensitization. They also state that vaccination remains standard of care in this population. - PMID:40160827

[D | guideline supported] The UK Kidney Association vascular access guideline emphasises planning access ahead, including education, vein preservation and timely assessment. It retains the fistula as the optimal access concept, framed as an individualised shared decision rather than 'fistula first' for everyone. (verified with caveat) - PMID:40813633

[D | emerging] COL4A5 defects account for most cases of post-transplant anti-GBM disease. Gene deletions are reported to be more commonly associated with the complication than point mutations. This implies, but does not quantify, lower risk for missense variants. - PMID:14717941

[D | emerging] Some Alport recipients develop anti-GBM antibodies without ever developing clinical nephritis. Standard anti-GBM ELISA can be negative in true cases, and Western blotting was reported as more sensitive and specific. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[D | emerging] There is no agreed protocol for treating or preventing post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis in Alport syndrome. Approaches reported include steroids with tacrolimus, azathioprine or ciclosporin, and plasmapheresis. Anti-T-cell therapy, longer-term plasma exchange and mycophenolate did not prevent graft loss in reported retransplant cases. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[D | evidence supported] An Alport transplant case series reports favorable recipient outcomes across inheritance types, with vascular and late antibody-mediated complications. It provides no outcome data for heterozygous carrier donors. - PMID:42076904

[D | emerging] COL4A5 gene deletions are more commonly associated with post-transplant anti-GBM disease than point mutations. A small German series observed anti-GBM antibodies after transplant in patients with a deletion and a splice-site mutation. - PMID:1450636, PMID:14717941

[D | emerging] After a first graft is lost to anti-GBM nephritis, recurrence with accelerated rejection on retransplantation is reported. Anti-T-cell therapy, plasma exchange and mycophenolate mofetil did not prevent graft loss in a retransplant case series. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934
[D | emerging] Standard anti-GBM ELISA may be negative in Alport post-transplant anti-GBM disease. Western blotting against α5(IV) NC1 was reported as more sensitive and specific. - PMID:14717941

[D | hypothesis] In a small series, X-linked Alport recipients had other graft-threatening events besides anti-GBM disease. One lost a graft to COVID-19-associated arterial thrombosis; another developed late antibody-mediated rejection at six years. - PMID:42076904

[D | hypothesis] Individual COL4A5 glycine substitutions have been reported as pathogenic: p.Gly624Asp was inherited from a hemizygous father with Alport syndrome, with familial segregation analysis performed, and p.Gly775Val arose de novo. p.Gly624Asp was described as usually associated with late-onset disease and variable renal involvement. - PMID:42881817, PMID:42905207

[D | hypothesis] Segregation evidence is weighed conservatively in Alport variant classification. In a COL4A3 splice variant, a phenotypically affected mother who did not carry the variant precluded supportive co-segregation, PP4 was not applied, and the variant remained a VUS despite functional splicing data. - PMID:42936413

[D | hypothesis] Computational assessment can place VUS in functionally critical domains and predict disruption, but sources treat this as supporting biological plausibility only. DNA-based testing is described as incompletely capturing splice and regulatory effects, and kidney RNA analysis is proposed to refine classification. - PMID:41901018, PMID:42614610

[D | emerging] Evidence for SGLT2 inhibitors (and MRAs) in Alport syndrome is limited and inconsistent. The Korean guideline makes no recommendation for routine use. Some reviews describe SGLT2i as an option for persistent albuminuria despite RAAS blockade, but none addresses advanced CKD. - PMID:39840589, PMID:42316418

[D | guideline supported] A guideline summary of KDIGO 2024 (secondary source, not the primary guideline text) reports that systematic correction of metabolic acidosis is no longer regarded as a nephroprotective measure. The summary gives no bicarbonate treatment threshold and no monitoring frequency. (verified with caveat) - PMID:40518893

[E | guideline supported] The guideline abstract gives standard-of-care therapy (early RAS blockade, with SGLT2 inhibitors in adults with proteinuria and CKD). It gives no recommendation on the timing or modality of kidney replacement therapy at eGFR <15. (verified with caveat) - PMID:39673454

[E | hypothesis] The sources contain no guideline criteria or eGFR thresholds for pre-emptive transplant referral or waitlisting, and no Alport-specific transplant outcome data. One single-centre study states as background that transplantation is the most effective treatment for end-stage kidney disease. - PMID:41327164

blocks.text: Abnormal domains: renal, electrolytes, haematologic

items: [C | evidence supported] Variant interpretation in Alport spectrum disorder is dynamic. On reassessment against ACMG criteria, 10 of 80 variants originally reported as disease-causing were downgraded to VUS. VUS cases had a significantly more limited phenotype than non-downgraded cases, and older (pre-ACMG era) genetic reports should be critically re-evaluated. - PMID:41851263

[D | emerging] In one adult case with a COL4A4 VUS, a 'probable' Alport syndrome diagnosis was supported by integrating phenotype, characteristic electron microscopy findings and compatible family history. The authors emphasise combining electron microscopy with genetic testing. - PMID:42774990

[C | evidence supported] Kidney biopsy is described as remaining the reference standard in pediatric podocyte and glomerular disease. A molecular result is said to change only a small, defined set of clinical decisions. - PMID:42942308

[C | emerging] RNA-based analyses (kidney transcriptome sequencing, minigene assays) can resolve the effects of splice-altering COL4A variants that DNA testing alone may not capture. Functional validation is described as necessary for non-canonical splice variants. - PMID:42404581, PMID:42614610

[C | evidence supported] KDIGO 2024, as interpreted for laboratories, calls for standardised creatinine and cystatin C measurement with traceability to international reference materials. It promotes combined creatinine–cystatin C eGFR for diagnostic accuracy. It encourages measured GFR with exogenous markers such as iohexol when eGFR may be inaccurate or clinically insufficient. - PMID:39584585

[C | evidence supported] In Indian participants with inulin-measured GFR, all creatinine-based eGFR equations overestimated GFR. CKD-EPIcys was not significantly different from measured GFR and had the lowest bias. - PMID:29390980

[C | evidence supported] KDIGO 2024 recommends equations combining creatinine and cystatin C for CKD diagnosis and staging. Cystatin C-inclusive equations show better bias, accuracy and prognostic value than creatinine-only equations. Cystatin C is particularly useful where creatinine is less reliable: hospitalisation, muscle-mass change, critical illness and medication dosing. - PMID:39902788, PMID:42424121

[C | emerging] In acute deterioration on established CKD, creatinine-based definitions show reduced prognostic accuracy. Cystatin C-based eGFR shows superior discrimination for mortality and progression. - PMID:42954720
[C | evidence supported] Expert guidelines recommend genetic testing as the gold standard for diagnosing Alport syndrome and for demonstrating its mode of inheritance. - PMID:23349312
[C | evidence supported] Guidelines call for identifying and following all affected members of a family with X-linked Alport syndrome, including most mothers of affected males. - PMID:23349312

[C | evidence supported] Guidelines discourage affected mothers of males with X-linked Alport syndrome from kidney donation because of their own risk of kidney failure. A case series similarly emphasises molecular confirmation and careful donor evaluation for transplantation in Alport syndrome. - PMID:23349312, PMID:42076904

[C | evidence supported] Alport syndrome is characterized by progressive hematuria, proteinuria and kidney failure, frequently accompanied by hearing loss and ocular abnormalities. This indirectly supports assessing hearing and eyes during evaluation, but no source specifies an examination protocol. - PMID:41853742, PMID:42316418
[E | evidence supported] The 2020 pediatric/young-adult recommendations include diagnostic tactics intended to ensure early diagnosis, but the abstract does not list them. - PMID:33159213

[B | guideline supported] A national nephrology society commentary on KDIGO 2017 suggests monitoring calcium, phosphate, PTH and alkaline phosphatase in adults with CKD G4 and recommends it in G5. It advises against this monitoring in G3. - PMID:32821415

[B | guideline supported] KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD guidance covers adults with CKD G3a-G5 and dialysis. It emphasises basing treatment on trends in laboratory values rather than a single abnormal result, and avoiding hypercalcaemia when treating secondary hyperparathyroidism. (verified with caveat) - PMID:29459980
[B | guideline supported] The same commentary advises against routine vitamin D deficiency screening (G3-G5), routine BMD testing (G4-G5) and routine bone biopsy in adults with CKD. - PMID:32821415

[C | guideline supported] ASN 2026 guidance emphasises longitudinal eGFR and albuminuria as foundational risk markers. It notes a role for cardiac biomarkers and imaging, and says the KFRE and PREVENT equations may help identify high-risk patients. It flags gaps for advanced CKD, younger individuals and glomerular disorders. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42684397

[D | guideline supported] The KDIGO 2022 hepatitis C in CKD guideline includes a chapter on detection and evaluation of HCV in CKD. It recommends sofosbuvir-based DAA treatment in G4-G5 including dialysis, and acceptance of HCV-positive donor kidneys. The abstract does not specify the screening recommendations. (verified with caveat) - PMID:38079642

[D | hypothesis] Ancillary functional or tissue evidence has been proposed to support COL4A5 variant interpretation. Absent α5(IV) staining in the epidermal basement membrane supports X-linked AS. A cell-based α345(IV) trimerization assay correlated with clinical severity and may help separate pathogenic from nonpathogenic missense variants. - PMID:19728970, PMID:32405592

[C | guideline supported] The 2024 ERKNet/ERA/ESPN guideline names joint genetic analysis of COL4A3/4/5 as the key diagnostic test when evaluating persistent haematuria, proteinuria or kidney failure of unknown origin. The abstract gives no clinical-only diagnostic criteria for when a definitive variant is absent. (verified with caveat) - PMID:39673454

[D | guideline supported] The guideline describes the COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy phenotype as persistent haematuria progressing to kidney replacement therapy, often with sensorineural deafness and occasionally ocular anomalies. These are the features a clinical assessment would examine. (verified with caveat) - PMID:39673454

[C | evidence supported] Alport syndrome expert guidance recommends genetic testing for persistent haematuria and cascade testing of first-degree family members. Family testing is also the mechanism for obtaining segregation evidence. - PMID:34930753

[D | emerging] In a COL4A4 case, a novel missense variant remained formally a VUS under ACMG/AMP criteria. Even so, phenotype, characteristic glomerular basement membrane ultrastructure and compatible family history were judged to strongly support it as the most likely molecular explanation. This illustrates that clinical and family evidence may support relevance without formal reclassification. - PMID:42774990

[C | emerging] Kidney transcriptome sequencing of biopsies with glomerular basement membrane abnormalities identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic COL4A variants that DNA testing alone did not readily resolve, particularly splice-altering ones. RNA analysis is therefore a complementary evidence line alongside segregation. - PMID:42614610

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports that the 2024 KDIGO guideline recommends combined creatinine–cystatin C equations for CKD diagnosis and staging. It also states that cystatin C-inclusive equations generally have better bias and accuracy than creatinine-only equations across diverse populations. No performance data are given for GFR below 15 mL/min/1.73m2. - PMID:42424121

[C | emerging] In 260 ADPKD patients compared against iothalamate-measured GFR, eGFRcys and eGFRcr-cys showed greater cross-sectional bias than eGFRcr. eGFRcr-cys had the highest precision, and its slopes agreed better with measured GFR decline. Results were not reported by GFR stage, and the disease (ADPKD) differs from this patient's. - PMID:42733501

[C | emerging] An older review raises concerns about non-renal influences on circulating cystatin C, particularly steroid therapy and possibly malignancy. Such factors could affect eGFRcys accuracy independently of GFR. - PMID:11928770

[D | hypothesis] In a large Chinese clinical population without measured GFR, different CKD-EPI equations produced substantial CKD-stage reclassification. Notably, eGFRcys reclassified 28.8% to a worse stage compared with 2009 eGFRcr. Equation choice can therefore change staging, but this study cannot say which equation is more accurate. - PMID:40978190

[C | guideline supported] The 2024 ERKNet/ERA/ESPN Alport guideline describes COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy as frequently associated with sensorineural deafness and occasionally with ocular anomalies. Audiologists and ophthalmologists were part of the guideline panel. The abstract does not state which baseline audiologic or ophthalmologic examinations are recommended. - PMID:39673454

[C | evidence supported] In autosomal dominant Alport syndrome (heterozygous COL4A3/COL4A4), the typical Alport hearing loss and ocular abnormalities are not present. Genetic testing distinguishes autosomal dominant from X-linked disease, which carries a higher risk of kidney failure. Documented extrarenal features would therefore be more consistent with a non-autosomal-dominant form, but this is an inference, not a validated diagnostic rule. - PMID:42172079

[C | evidence supported] A classical Alport phenotype is described in consensus and expert-guideline sources: haematuria and renal failure, with a family history of haematuria or renal failure. These are the traditional indications for COL4A3-5 testing. - PMID:33854215, PMID:34930753

[C | evidence supported] Hearing loss, retinopathy and lamellated GBM (on biopsy) are listed alongside renal failure as features prompting clinical or biopsy suspicion of Alport syndrome. One cohort refers to 'standard diagnostic criteria of AS' and found pathogenic variants in more than half of patients meeting fewer than three of them. The criteria themselves are not enumerated in these abstracts. - PMID:25307543, PMID:27627812

[D | emerging] Clinical and pathological diagnostic criteria have been applied to diagnose Alport syndrome when genetic testing returned only a COL4A3-5 VUS. In one paediatric series, children were included as meeting established clinical and pathological criteria despite VUS results. In a case report, phenotype plus characteristic EM findings plus family history supported a 'probable' diagnosis despite a VUS. - PMID:41908531, PMID:42774990

[C | evidence supported] In a multi-laboratory variant series, the average age at end-stage renal failure for COL4A5 variants was about 24 years. Renal failure occurred sooner with non-missense than with missense COL4A5 variants. - PMID:27627812

[C | evidence supported] Alport syndrome genetic-testing guidance advocates cascade testing of first-degree family members once a COL4A3–COL4A5 variant is identified. This gives a clinical rationale for testing maternal relatives, but the source does not specify how segregation results change variant classification. - PMID:34930753

[C | evidence supported] KDIGO eGFR categories define G5 as eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m2 in people not on kidney replacement therapy. The patient's latest CKD-EPI 2021 eGFR of 6.2 mL/min/1.73 m2 falls in this category. - PMID:34571286

[C | emerging] A rapid fall in eGFR in someone with established CKD fits the reviewed concept of acute-on-chronic kidney disease. That review reports creatinine-based definitions are less accurate prognostically in CKD, while cystatin C-based eGFR discriminates mortality and progression better. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] In a CKD cohort, a large positive difference between creatinine-based and cystatin C-based eGFR was associated with higher MACE risk and faster coronary artery calcification progression. This is an association, not proof of causation. - PMID:34571286

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalemia is defined as serum potassium greater than 5.0 mEq/L and hypokalemia as less than 3.5 mEq/L. The patient's latest K of 5.2 mmol/L exceeds this hyperkalemia threshold (mild range). - PMID:36689973

[C | evidence supported] Emergent hyperkalemia treatment is recommended for clinical signs or symptoms (e.g., muscle weakness, paralysis) or ECG abnormalities. ECG may not correlate with serum potassium. Dialysis may be considered in end-stage renal disease or severe renal impairment. - PMID:36689973
