Verified research findings (265)

items: [A | established] In non-dialysis CKD 3-5, ARB monotherapy raised the odds of hyperkalaemia 2.08-5.10-fold versus placebo and CCBs. RAAS inhibitor-associated hyperkalaemia often leads to dose reduction or stopping. - PMID:32333236, PMID:40542996

[A | established] In adults with CKD, darbepoetin alfa probably reduces blood transfusions versus placebo (moderate certainty). Epoetin alfa and epoetin beta may reduce transfusions (low certainty). - PMID:36791280

[A | established] ESAs have not been shown to reduce all-cause mortality: darbepoetin alfa probably has no effect versus placebo, and effects are uncertain for the other ESAs. Effects on cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, kidney failure and fatigue were uncertain. - PMID:36791280

[A | established] ESAs probably or possibly increase hypertension versus placebo, and the epoetin alfa label lists uncontrolled hypertension as a contraindication. - DB:cd2336d47c9cd2c2, PMID:36791280

[A | evidence supported] In a Cochrane meta-analysis of 6 RCTs (7,348 participants with hypertension and CKD), lower BP targets (130/80 or below) versus standard targets probably made little to no difference to total mortality, serious adverse events or cardiovascular events. They may make little to no difference to progression to ESRD. - PMID:39403990

[A | established] An international Alport syndrome guideline (ERKNet/ERA/ESPN, based on systematic literature review and graded consensus) states that early renin-angiotensin system blockade is the standard of care for COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy. It adds that SGLT2 inhibitors may be added in adults with proteinuria and CKD. - PMID:39673454

[A | guideline supported] The guideline advises that relatives with heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 variants should be considered only as a last resort for living kidney donation. This is relevant to kidney replacement planning, but it does not bear directly on RAS or BP outcomes. - PMID:39673454

[A | guideline supported] The 2024 international Alport guideline (ERKNet/ERA/ESPN) states that early RAS blockade is standard-of-care therapy for COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy. It also states that SGLT2 inhibitors may be added in adults with proteinuria and CKD. - PMID:39673454

[A | guideline supported] A 2026 GRADE-based systematic review and guideline found that early RAS blockade delays progression to kidney failure and improves survival, with the greatest benefit when started at the microscopic haematuria or microalbuminuria stage. It strongly recommends early RAS blockade and makes no recommendation for routine cyclosporine, MRAs or SGLT2 inhibitors. - PMID:42316418

[A | guideline supported] Disease-specific guidance relevant to kidney replacement planning has two parts. First, heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 relatives should only be the last possible resource for living kidney donation. Second, variants of uncertain significance should not by themselves determine treatment or donor eligibility. - PMID:39673454, PMID:42792963
[A | established] Early renin-angiotensin system blockade is the guideline-endorsed standard of care for COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy, including Alport syndrome. - PMID:39673454, PMID:42316418

[A | guideline supported] For patients approaching kidney replacement therapy, the ERKNet guideline advises that relatives with heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 variants be considered only as a last-resort living kidney donor source. - PMID:39673454

[A | guideline supported] An international ERKNet/ERA/ESPN guideline, based on a systematic literature review and graded consensus, states that early RAS blockade is the standard of care in COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy including Alport syndrome. It states SGLT2 inhibitors may be added in adults with proteinuria and CKD. The abstract emphasises early initiation and does not specify recommendations for CKD G5. - PMID:39673454

[B | evidence supported] In an individual-participant meta-analysis of RCTs in adults with baseline eGFR <30, initiating an ACEi or ARB lowered the risk of kidney failure with replacement therapy but did not significantly change death before KFRT. No significant interaction was found by eGFR subgroup (<20 vs ≥20) or by albuminuria. - PMID:38950402

[B | evidence supported] In the STOP-ACEi RCT (advanced, progressive CKD, eGFR <30), discontinuing RAS inhibitors did not significantly change eGFR at 3 years compared with continuing them. ESKD/KRT was numerically more frequent after discontinuation (non-significant), and cardiovascular events and deaths were similar. - PMID:36326117

[B | evidence supported] In an individual-participant meta-analysis of 18 RCTs in advanced CKD (baseline eGFR <30), starting an ACEi or ARB lowered the risk of KFRT but not death. Patient-level hyperkalaemia and AKI data were not available. - PMID:38950402

[B | evidence supported] Network meta-analyses disagree on ARB benefit in CKD. One found ARBs reduced kidney failure versus placebo (OR 0.70). The other, in non-dialysis CKD 3-5, found ARB monotherapy no better than CCBs, beta-blockers or diuretics on primary outcomes. Both ranked ACEi above ARB. - PMID:26597926, PMID:32333236

[B | emerging] In a meta-analysis of RCTs in CKD or heart failure, novel potassium binders improved RAAS inhibitor optimisation versus placebo, decreased hyperkalaemia incidence by 28% and lowered potassium by 0.71 mEq/L. In CREDENCE and DAPA-CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors lowered the risk of RAS blockade discontinuation by 15%. - PMID:37876229, PMID:40542996

[B | evidence supported] In an RCT of stage 4 CKD with poorly controlled hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring, chlorthalidone lowered 24-h ambulatory systolic BP versus placebo. It also lowered albuminuria at 12 weeks. Outcomes were surrogate only, and baseline eGFR (~23) was well above this patient's. - PMID:34739197
[B | evidence supported] In the same trial, chlorthalidone increased hypokalemia, reversible serum creatinine rises, hyperglycemia, dizziness and hyperuricemia compared with placebo. - PMID:34739197

[B | evidence supported] In diabetic CKD, a meta-analysis of 17 RCTs found that SGLT2 inhibitors modestly lowered systolic BP. They increased volume depletion-related adverse events and had neutral short- to medium-term effects on eGFR and albuminuria. - PMID:42826278

[B | evidence supported] In a cluster RCT, home BP telemonitoring with pharmacist case management improved BP control versus usual care over 12 months, and the benefit persisted 6 months after the intervention ended. - PMID:23821088

[B | evidence supported] Iron status affects ESA need. Proactive high-dose IV iron in haemodialysis reduced cardiovascular/death events and ESA dose versus reactive low-dose iron. In non-dialysis CKD with iron deficiency, IV ferric carboxymaltose (ferritin target 400–600 µg/L) delayed or reduced the need for ESAs versus oral iron. - PMID:24891437, PMID:30365356

[B | evidence supported] Oral HIF prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors are alternatives evaluated against ESAs. Daprodustat was noninferior to ESAs for Hb change and MACE in both dialysis and non-dialysis CKD. Roxadustat was noninferior to epoetin alfa for Hb in dialysis CKD, with a comparable adverse-event profile. - PMID:34739194, PMID:34739196, PMID:35361724

[B | evidence supported] In adults on maintenance haemodialysis, a proactive high-dose IV iron sucrose regimen was superior to a reactive low-dose regimen. It reduced the composite of nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, heart-failure hospitalisation or death, and lowered the ESA dose required. - PMID:30365356

[B | evidence supported] In non-dialysis CKD with anaemia and iron deficiency not receiving ESAs, IV ferric carboxymaltose targeting a higher ferritin delayed or reduced the need for other anaemia management (ESA, other iron or transfusion) compared with oral iron. It also produced a greater Hb rise. - PMID:24891437

[B | evidence supported] Safety in CKD trials: FIND-CKD reported similar adverse event and serious adverse event rates across arms, with no renal toxicity and no difference in cardiovascular or infectious events. PIVOTAL reported equal infection rates between the high-dose and low-dose IV iron arms. - PMID:24891437, PMID:30365356

[B | evidence supported] For newer potassium binders in CKD, a Cochrane systematic review found low-certainty evidence of little or no effect on all-cause death. No included study reported cardiac arrhythmias or major GI events, so benefit on patient-important outcomes is unproven. - PMID:32588430

[B | evidence supported] Potassium binders lower serum potassium modestly in CKD: about 0.6-0.7 mEq/L on pooled estimates. Newer binders also reduced the incidence of hyperkalaemia. - PMID:32588430, PMID:40542996

[B | evidence supported] Newer binders improved the ability to start or maintain RAAS-inhibitor therapy versus placebo. In the AMBER RCT, patiromer allowed more patients with CKD and resistant hypertension to continue spironolactone. AMBER enrolled only eGFR 25-45. - PMID:31533906, PMID:40542996

[B | guideline supported] For relatives of Alport patients, the 2024 ERKNet/ERA/ESPN guideline states that heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 carriers should only be the last possible resource for living kidney donation. The guideline positions joint COL4A3/4/5 genetic testing as the key diagnostic test. - PMID:39673454

[B | guideline supported] Renin-angiotensin system blockade is the guideline standard of care in Alport syndrome, and SGLT2 inhibitors may be added in adults with proteinuria and CKD. Their role and safety at eGFR around 6 are not addressed in these sources. - PMID:39673454

[B | evidence supported] In randomized trials of people with CKD and diabetes, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced kidney failure, all-cause death and heart-failure hospitalisation versus placebo. No studies included people treated with dialysis. - PMID:38770818

[B | evidence supported] In diabetic CKD trials, SGLT2 inhibitors increased volume depletion-related adverse events but did not significantly increase urinary tract infections. The label also notes a higher incidence of volume-depletion reactions in renal impairment. - DB:24ee21044a5cb6d1, PMID:42826278

[B | emerging] Across 85 RCTs, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with a small increase in haemoglobin (~0.6 g/dL versus control) and a small decrease in transferrin saturation. The clinical significance of these changes is unclear. - PMID:42925557

[B | evidence supported] In IgA nephropathy (PROTECT, phase 3 RCT), sparsentan slowed eGFR decline and kept proteinuria lower versus maximally titrated irbesartan over 110 weeks. The composite kidney failure endpoint occurred numerically less often (9% vs 13%). Sparsentan is FDA/EMA approved for IgAN. - PMID:37931634, PMID:42483539

[B | evidence supported] The FDA label carries a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity and requires a REMS programme. Transaminases and bilirubin should be measured before initiation and every 3 months. Treatment should be interrupted if aminotransferases exceed 3 times ULN, and co-administration with ARBs, ERAs or aliskiren is contraindicated. - DB:92394967110d9b29, PMID:42769334

[B | evidence supported] In SONAR, adults with type 2 diabetes, eGFR 25-75 and UACR 300-5000 mg/g who responded during an enrichment phase had a lower risk of a composite renal endpoint on atrasentan than on placebo (HR 0.65). - PMID:30995972

[B | evidence supported] Atrasentan increased fluid retention and anaemia adverse events in SONAR. Hospitalisation for heart failure was numerically higher but not statistically significant. - PMID:30995972, PMID:42222077

[B | evidence supported] In patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, a prespecified pooled analysis of two phase 3 RCTs (FIDELITY, n=13,026) found finerenone reduced composite cardiovascular and kidney outcomes versus placebo. - PMID:35023547

[B | evidence supported] Hyperkalaemia is the consistent safety signal with finerenone across trials and meta-analysis. It leads to more treatment discontinuation than placebo, while acute kidney injury was not increased in the meta-analysis. - PMID:35023547, PMID:41780000, PMID:42864264
[B | evidence supported] In FINE-ONE, finerenone caused a larger early eGFR fall than placebo over 6 months. eGFR values approached baseline after washout. - PMID:41780000

[B | guideline supported] The 2023 ESH guideline, endorsed by ERA, recommends an office BP target below 130/80 mmHg in most CKD patients and recommends against an office target below 120/70 mmHg in all CKD patients. The recommendation is not specific to CKD G5 or dialysis. - PMID:38365947

[B | guideline supported] The eligibility criteria stated in the ESH guideline for disease-modifying agents are SGLT2 inhibitors at eGFR 20 or above, and finerenone with type 2 diabetes, albuminuria, eGFR 25 or above and potassium below 5.0. The patient's current values (eGFR 6.2, K 5.2, no recorded diabetes) fall outside these criteria. - PMID:38365947

[B | guideline supported] Cardio-kidney protective drug classes have mostly been tested at eGFR of 20 or more. Guidance identifies advanced CKD, dialysis, younger patients and glomerular disorders as gaps where data are limited. - PMID:42684397, PMID:42942386

[B | evidence supported] In Alport syndrome, cyclosporine and MRAs reduced proteinuria only in the short term, without sustained renoprotection. Cyclosporine carries a substantial nephrotoxicity risk. This is the only explicit nephrotoxin-related statement in the provided sources. - PMID:42316418

[B | guideline supported] KDOQI 2020 recommends a dietary protein record of 0.55-0.6 g/kg/day for CKD patients without diabetes and 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day for diabetic kidney disease (non-dialysis context). - PMID:32737016
[B | guideline supported] Patients with CKD should be referred to registered dietitians (or the regional equivalent) for individualised medical nutrition therapy. - PMID:32737016

[B | evidence supported] Meta-analyses of RCTs in peritoneal dialysis patients show that long-term (≥12 months) ACEi/ARB use modestly slows the decline of residual kidney function compared with placebo or other antihypertensives; short-term use showed no significant benefit. - PMID:24953826, PMID:33029520
[B | emerging] One RCT included in the Cochrane review found that long-term ramipril versus other antihypertensives delayed progression to complete anuria in CAPD patients. - PMID:24953826
[B | evidence supported] In PD RCTs, ACEi/ARB use was not associated with a significant difference in serum potassium compared with control groups. - PMID:24953826, PMID:33029520

[B | evidence supported] Across dialysis populations (HD and PD), ACEi/ARB therapy showed no significant effect on all-cause mortality or cardiovascular death in pooled RCTs. ARBs were associated with fewer heart failure events, and drug-related adverse events did not differ. - PMID:28666408

[B | evidence supported] The Cochrane review concluded that the evidence is insufficient to support ACEi/ARB as first-line antihypertensive therapy in PD. A PD hypertension review places antihypertensive drugs second-line after volume management. - PMID:24953826, PMID:30341090

[B | guideline supported] Human evidence indicates that the timing of RAS blockade matters. Earlier initiation (microscopic hematuria or microalbuminuria stage) is associated with greatest delay to kidney failure and improved survival. This is based mostly on retrospective/observational data. - PMID:35547199, PMID:40165927, PMID:42316418

[B | evidence supported] In a retrospective registry of 101 patients with autosomal recessive Alport syndrome, RAAS inhibition was associated with later CKD5 onset across disease stages. Median age at CKD5 was 24 years untreated versus 35 years when treatment started at the impaired-kidney-function steps (T-III). No patient treated from the microalbuminuria stage progressed to CKD5. The magnitude of benefit is undefined for initiation at the proteinuria stage because of few events. - PMID:33772369
[B | guideline supported] The guideline states that relatives with heterozygous COL4A3/4/5 variants should be considered only as the last possible resource for living kidney donation. - PMID:39673454

[B | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of 19 RCTs (3627 patients), both SZC and patiromer lowered serum potassium by end of treatment. Only SZC produced a significant reduction in the first 48-72 hours. - PMID:41811379

[B | evidence supported] In pooled RCT data, patiromer enabled RAASi optimization (target dosing, fewer discontinuations due to hyperkalemia). SZC normalized potassium and reduced hyperkalemia incidence. These are process and surrogate outcomes, not hard clinical endpoints. - PMID:41811379

[B | evidence supported] In the AMBER RCT (resistant hypertension with CKD), patiromer increased persistent spironolactone use. This held in the prespecified eGFR 25 to <30 subgroup (84% vs 56%), with comparable safety across eGFR subgroups. The endpoint was continued drug use and blood pressure, not clinical outcomes. - PMID:35369022
[B | evidence supported] Safety differs by agent: SZC is associated with more edema, and patiromer with more constipation and hypokalemia. - PMID:41811379

[B | evidence supported] In PD (CAPD) patients, long-term (12 months or more) ARB use preserved residual kidney function compared with other antihypertensives, but short-term use (six months or less) did not. Long-term ramipril reduced RKF decline and delayed progression to complete anuria. - PMID:24953826

[B | evidence supported] Two independent meta-analyses agree that ACEi or ARB use slows loss of residual renal function in dialysis, predominantly in PD. One also reported slower decline in urine volume. - PMID:19776050, PMID:28666408

[B | evidence supported] In PD trials, ACEi or ARB use did not reduce mortality or cardiovascular events. One dialysis meta-analysis suggested ARBs may reduce heart failure events, but showed no all-cause mortality difference. - PMID:19776050, PMID:24953826, PMID:28666408

[B | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of RCTs in CKD stage 4-5 (eGFR ≤30), RAAS blockade was associated with reduced progression to ESKD but showed no benefit on all-cause mortality or MACE. The authors concluded it may be considered in selected patients. - PMID:38458564

[B | evidence supported] In a target-trial emulation of adults with eGFR <30 already treated with RAS inhibitors, discontinuation was associated with higher 3-year risk of major cardiovascular events (adjusted RR 2.02) and of kidney replacement therapy initiation (adjusted RR 1.34) compared with continuation. The authors conclude that the risk-benefit balance favours continued use with close monitoring. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] Alport syndrome reviews and a genetic case series state that kidney management centres on early ACE-inhibitor initiation and that very early RAAS blockade can delay kidney failure. - PMID:36553470, PMID:37122389

[C | evidence supported] Uptake of RAAS inhibitors in CKD is limited by fear of hyperkalaemia and worsening kidney function, and pivotal HFrEF ACEi trials excluded people with creatinine at or above about 2.5 mg/dL. Hyperkalaemia data were not available in the advanced-CKD meta-analysis. - PMID:33495289, PMID:38950402

[C | emerging] In a small retrospective predialysis CKD cohort, time-dependent ACEi/ARB use was not significantly associated with major adverse kidney or cardiovascular events. Albuminuria severity and lower eGFR were strong risk markers. - PMID:42942488

[C | emerging] The genetic basis is unconfirmed: the COL4A5 p.Gly1048Glu variant is classified as a VUS, so X-linked Alport is a clinical and pedigree diagnosis. Genetic testing distinguishes X-linked from autosomal forms and can change management. - PMID:36553470, PMID:42172079

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review of Alport syndrome states that ACEi, or an ARB if ACEi is not tolerated, slows kidney disease progression and can delay kidney failure by years. It also states there is no specific curative treatment. - PMID:38745975

[C | evidence supported] Alport-specific observational data are mixed. In 108 Indian children with COL4A variants, ACEi/ARB showed no significant impact on proteinuria or CKD at 5-year follow-up. In the CARDINAL trial, eGFR declined about 4.9 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year despite 78% of participants receiving ACEi or ARB. - PMID:33789284, PMID:42955332

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review reports that KDIGO 2021 accepted a lower systolic BP target following SPRINT. It also states that intensive SBP targeting (<120 mmHg) is controversial in CKD and that no RCTs have enrolled only CKD patients, particularly advanced CKD. - PMID:34153181
[C | emerging] The same review states that a lower SBP target is associated with a higher risk of adverse kidney outcomes in CKD. - PMID:34153181

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review of Alport syndrome names regular monitoring of kidney function and BP, with medication to control hypertension, as crucial parts of management. - PMID:38021591

[C | hypothesis] An observational case-control study found microvascular/hypertensive retinopathy more common and more severe in X-linked and autosomal recessive Alport syndrome than in normotensive controls. The authors suggest that improved BP may slow renal decline in Alport syndrome. A single case report describes severe vision loss with optic disc and macular edema in a woman with X-linked Alport and uncontrolled hypertension. - PMID:30985254, PMID:41657422
[C | evidence supported] A review states that RAS inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors slow kidney disease progression and reduce heart failure complications for most patients with CKD. - PMID:39986466
[C | emerging] In older adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD, a systematic review reports that sodium restriction reduced BP and albuminuria. - PMID:42819067

[C | emerging] A CKD source states, as background rather than as a study result, that optimal CKD management includes avoiding potential nephrotoxins and adjusting drug doses. It provides no outcome data supporting this. - PMID:40160047

[C | emerging] The same CKD source states that CKD patients require monitoring for complications including hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphataemia, vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism and anaemia. - PMID:40160047

[C | guideline supported] Older guidance recommends dietary sodium limitation in hypertensive patients, including those with CKD: 65–100 mmol/day (CHEP 2007) or no more than 2 g/day (2005 review). - PMID:16298269, PMID:17534460

[C | evidence supported] In a systematic review of older adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD, sodium restriction reduced blood pressure and albuminuria. Moderated protein record was associated with favourable renal outcomes when nutritional status was monitored. - PMID:42819067

[C | emerging] For protein restriction, the MDRD trial failed to show a benefit on its primary outcome of GFR decline. Later meta-analyses and RCTs suggest that ketoanalogue-supplemented low or very-low protein diets may reduce GFR loss in adherent, rapidly progressing patients, in addition to RAAS inhibition. - PMID:31484354
[C | emerging] Ketoanalogue-supplemented low or very-low protein diets appear nutritionally safe, but how muscle protein metabolism adapts to them remains largely unknown. - PMID:31484354

[C | evidence supported] Evidence for specific protein or salt record thresholds in CKD is described as far from compelling. Long-term adherence is a key barrier. It is uncertain whether these diets add benefit alongside newer therapies such as SGLT2 inhibitors or non-steroidal MRAs. - PMID:37915942

[C | evidence supported] In hypertensive CKD, a 2026 narrative review recommends individualised potassium management rather than universal restriction of fruits and vegetables. It reports that KDIGO 2024 emphasises limiting foods rich in bioavailable potassium, especially processed foods, with serum potassium monitored according to baseline risk. - PMID:42650632

[C | guideline supported] A blood pressure goal of <130/80 mmHg for CKD patients is stated by both the NKF guideline (cited in a 2005 review) and CHEP 2007. Dietary sodium restriction is part of the non-pharmacological route to this goal. - PMID:16298269, PMID:17534460

[C | emerging] In haemodialysis patients (target trial emulation), an Hb target of 105–125 g/L under controlled darbepoetin dosing was not associated with higher mortality than 95–115 g/L. Targets above 125 g/L may increase mortality. - PMID:42893801

[C | emerging] ESA cardiovascular risk appears concentrated in hyporesponders needing high doses or treated to high Hb targets. In pre-dialysis CKD, lower 1,25(OH)2D was independently associated with ESA hyporesponsiveness (association only). - PMID:42794474, PMID:42795843

[C | evidence supported] Guideline position as described in a 2026 review: contemporary guidelines recommend iron therapy in CKD only when anaemia is present. Iron (oral and IV) combined with ESAs is described as the traditional treatment of CKD anaemia. - PMID:42640172, PMID:42795843

[C | evidence supported] In adults with anaemia but without CKD, very low-quality evidence suggests oral iron may reduce transfusion need, with no demonstrated mortality benefit. IV iron gave a modest Hb rise without clinical benefit. Oral iron caused mostly mild GI adverse effects, and no trials reported severe allergic reactions to parenteral iron. - PMID:25550190

[C | emerging] A review reports that IV iron improved symptoms in heart failure with CKD stage 3, and that high-dose iron reduced heart-failure hospitalisations by 44% in dialysis patients. - PMID:33495289

[C | evidence supported] Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has reported serious adverse effects, including colonic necrosis, hypomagnesaemia and hypernatraemia. The newer binders are described as having a more favourable safety profile, although GI effects in RCTs remain uncertain. - PMID:31668450, PMID:32588430, PMID:38173862

[C | emerging] Sodium-exchanging versus calcium-exchanging resins differ in volume effects: calcium polystyrene sulfonate is described as avoiding hypervolaemia because it exchanges calcium rather than sodium for potassium. - PMID:31338108

[C | emerging] Potassium binders may have a role in preventing hyperkalaemia in patients on haemodialysis, especially across long interdialytic intervals, but long-term confirmation is needed. - PMID:31668450

[C | evidence supported] Guideline position is reported only second-hand. The meta-analysis states novel binders are recommended by current guidelines for hyperkalaemia, and a letter references KDIGO 2021 binder prioritisation. No guideline text was provided. - PMID:40542996, PMID:42626019

[C | emerging] In real-world Italian data, patiromer users had higher adherence than users of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate or sodium polystyrene sulfonate, along with fewer HF-related events. This is an association; the authors state that randomized confirmation is needed. - PMID:42509402

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalaemia risk rises as GFR declines, and with high potassium record, diabetes, heart failure and RAAS blockade. Monitoring frameworks emphasise baseline risk stratification, early potassium surveillance and correction of reversible triggers. - PMID:31338108, PMID:42741732

[C | evidence supported] In a UK advanced kidney care cohort, patients were routinely referred to pre-dialysis/KRT planning services once eGFR fell below 20 mL/min/1.73m2. This patient's eGFR (6.2) and rapid decline place him well beyond that referral point. - PMID:40755968

[C | evidence supported] In the same cohort, pre-emptive transplantation was associated with markedly higher 5-year survival than haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. Younger patients (<50 years) had high survival. A substantial fraction of those opting for KRT died before reaching it. - PMID:40755968

[C | evidence supported] Early identification of at-risk relatives is described as a priority in Alport syndrome. Genetic testing reveals the inheritance pattern, which bears on both family screening and donor selection. - PMID:38745975

[C | evidence supported] Tunneled dialysis catheters are associated with bloodstream infection, central venous injury and mortality. Arteriovenous fistulas offer the best long-term value when creation is risk-based and the fistula matures and is used. Peritoneal dialysis is underutilised despite comparable outcomes in many cohorts. - PMID:41957978

[C | evidence supported] For access monitoring, the review supports selective preoperative imaging, targeted duplex ultrasound and ultrasound-guided cannulation rather than routine surveillance. AVGs may suit selected patients by shortening catheter exposure, at the cost of more reinterventions. - PMID:41957978

[C | evidence supported] Post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis is reported in roughly up to 5% of Alport syndrome transplant recipients and is immunologically distinct from classical Goodpasture disease. In X-linked Alport syndrome the usual alloantigen target is alpha5(IV), because the intact donor GBM presents a non-tolerised antigen. - PMID:14717941, PMID:28515156, PMID:42390934

[C | evidence supported] When anti-GBM nephritis occurs, allograft failure typically happens within weeks to months and usually within the first post-transplant year. Progression to graft loss is often rapid. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[C | emerging] There is no agreed treatment or prophylaxis protocol for post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis in Alport syndrome. Reported strategies vary and include steroids with calcineurin inhibitors or azathioprine, plus plasmapheresis to remove antibodies. - PMID:42390934

[C | evidence supported] Heterozygous female carriers of X-linked Alport syndrome have widely variable kidney outcomes, ranging from normal urinalysis to kidney failure and deafness. This is relevant when considering the mother or other female maternal relatives as living donors. - PMID:21380623

[C | evidence supported] Variants of uncertain significance should not independently determine treatment or donor eligibility. Molecular diagnosis enables cascade testing and safer assessment of living-related donors. - PMID:42792963

[C | evidence supported] Cascade screening of first-degree relatives of Alport patients identifies previously unrecognised disease. Among molecularly positive relatives in one cohort, 36.5% had proteinuria above 0.1 g/g and 13.5% had eGFR below 60. Genetic testing of all first-degree relatives is recommended regardless of hematuria. - PMID:42172079, PMID:42529192

[C | evidence supported] Genetic testing distinguishes X-linked from autosomal dominant Alport syndrome. X-linked disease carries a higher risk of kidney failure, which is relevant to genotype-specific prognosis and to interpreting relatives' risk. - PMID:42172079

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews state that the kidney-protective effects of SGLT2 inhibitors extend to people without type 2 diabetes. They cite dedicated renal trials (CREDENCE, DAPA-CKD, EMPA-KIDNEY) but give no quantitative non-diabetic estimates. - PMID:35113333, PMID:42778649

[C | evidence supported] At very low kidney function the sources advise against starting SGLT2 inhibitors. The dapagliflozin label does not recommend initiation below eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m2. A review discourages initiation at very low GFR because of an initial GFR dip and advises stopping during acute renal events, hypovolaemia or hypotension. - DB:24ee21044a5cb6d1, PMID:35113333

[C | emerging] A narrative review states that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce hyperkalaemia and fluid retention, which may improve the tolerability of other kidney therapies used in combination. - PMID:39907542

[C | emerging] In the FSGS phase 3 DUPLEX trial, 7.7% of participants carried P/LP COL4A3/4/5 variants. Enrolled patients spanned CKD stages 1 to 3b, with UP/C of at least 1.5 g/g. Sparsentan reduced proteinuria versus irbesartan but did not show a statistically significant eGFR-preservation benefit. - PMID:38765567, PMID:42433793

[C | evidence supported] Reviews report hyperkalemia and hypotension with sparsentan, and fluid retention/edema and anemia as endothelin receptor antagonist class risks requiring early surveillance. These risks are pertinent to a patient with K 5.2 mmol/L, Hb 10.4 g/dL and eGFR 6.2. - PMID:42433793, PMID:42644854

[C | emerging] In a post hoc SONAR analysis, atrasentan significantly reduced the composite kidney outcome in women but not in men. Women also had higher drug exposure and numerically more heart-failure events. - PMID:39661119

[C | emerging] In IgA nephropathy, atrasentan has accelerated or conditional approval based on proteinuria reduction. Full approval awaits kidney-function data, and the final ALIGN week-136 eGFR contrast was not statistically significant. - PMID:42483540, PMID:42644854

[C | evidence supported] Reviews recommend early surveillance for edema, anemia, liver-test abnormalities and pregnancy risk with endothelin receptor antagonists, with interruption if significant volume expansion occurs. The label carries a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity. - DB:8c5b2b2235bad05b, PMID:42644854

[C | emerging] In non-diabetic proteinuric CKD, a narrative review reports that the phase 3 FIND-CKD trial showed finerenone slows eGFR decline. The trial population was mainly glomerulonephritis and hypertensive nephropathy, and Alport syndrome is not described. - PMID:38858818, PMID:42469710

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews recommend structured potassium monitoring with finerenone: baseline risk stratification, early potassium surveillance, and correction of reversible triggers. - PMID:42741732

[C | emerging] Network meta-analyses suggest SGLT2 inhibitors and finerenone are complementary. Indirect comparisons favouring SGLT2 inhibitors for kidney outcomes are low certainty and hypothesis-generating. - PMID:42864264
[C | emerging] In diabetic CKD, early albuminuria reduction mediated much of finerenone's kidney benefit. The authors state this is not readily extendable to other drugs. - PMID:38048573

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews report that residual kidney function is associated with better survival, less morbidity and better quality of life in PD and HD patients. This is an association; the mechanism is unclear. - PMID:27182000, PMID:31630148, PMID:37781547

[C | emerging] A narrative review of PD recommends using ACE inhibitors and ARBs where possible to preserve RKF. A second review lists RAAS blockade among RKF-preservation strategies for HD and PD, but says the roles of blood pressure control and other factors are not clearly established. - PMID:31630148, PMID:37781547

[C | emerging] An HD-focused review proposes RKF-preservation measures that do not specifically include ACE inhibitors: monitoring urine volume and residual urea clearance, avoiding nephrotoxins, tighter hypertension control, minimising intradialytic hypotension, and considering incremental dialysis. - PMID:27182000

[C | emerging] In a retrospective cohort of 263 predialysis CKD adults, time-dependent ACE inhibitor/ARB use was not significantly associated with major adverse kidney events or cardiovascular events. Lower eGFR and greater albuminuria were associated with kidney events. - PMID:42942488

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalaemia is common in CKD and is described as a limiting factor for prescribing and up-titrating RAAS inhibitors. It is also independently associated with adverse outcomes and potentially lethal arrhythmia. - PMID:34227913, PMID:34313978

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews propose that newer potassium binders (patiromer, SZC) can manage and prevent hyperkalaemia and allow continuation of RAASi and MRA therapy. SZC is described as safe for chronic use based on 1 year of data. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is described as having limited efficacy evidence, and its chronic use is not routinely recommended because of toxicity concerns. - PMID:34227913, PMID:40841869

[C | emerging] In a 16-patient randomised crossover noninferiority trial in advanced CKD patients on RAAS inhibitors, a potassium-rich diet did not significantly raise serum potassium at 6 weeks. The two hyperkalaemia episodes were managed with SZC, allowing continuation of both diet and RAAS inhibition. - PMID:42636918
[C | evidence supported] Non-binder strategies described for reducing hyperkalaemia risk:
Combining SGLT2 inhibitors with RAASi.
Correcting constipation and metabolic acidosis.
Reviewing potassium-raising medications and additives.
Individualised, food-source-aware potassium management rather than reflexive restriction of fruits and vegetables. One review attributes this approach to KDIGO 2024. - PMID:40841869, PMID:42650632

[C | evidence supported] The trial evidence cited for SGLT2 inhibitor cardiorenal benefit extends to eGFR values down to 20 mL/min/1.73 m2. A separate review notes that MR antagonists are often introduced late, when reduced renal function raises hyperkalaemia risk and limits preventive benefit. - PMID:42733634, PMID:42942386

[C | emerging] In a large US claims cohort of CKD patients without baseline hyperkalaemia, 1.43% developed incident hyperkalaemia over 12 months. Those affected had higher comorbidity and greater RAASi use. A claims-based prediction model achieved an AUC of 0.843. - PMID:33204127
[C | evidence supported] In an RCT meta-analysis of CKD stage 4-5 patients, RAAS blockade reduced progression to ESKD. It did not reduce all-cause mortality or MACE. - PMID:38458564

[C | emerging] In observational analyses of advanced CKD, stopping RAS inhibitors was associated with more MACE and more kidney replacement therapy initiation than continuing them. This is an association, not proof of causation. - PMID:37214072, PMID:42851449
[C | emerging] A KDIGO conference report states that evidence for RAAS inhibitors and related therapies in advanced CKD remains limited. - PMID:41791738

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews consistently describe RAAS blockade as the foundation of Alport syndrome treatment to delay kidney failure. One describes the supporting evidence as strong. RAAS blockade does not target the underlying collagen IV defect. - PMID:39429698, PMID:41243004

[C | evidence supported] An adult nephrology clinic review positions ACE inhibitors as the default RAAS agent and ARBs as the alternative when an ACEi is not tolerated. It states that this approach slows progression and can delay kidney failure by years. The ARB is framed as a tolerability substitute, not as a comparatively tested equivalent. - PMID:38745975

[C | emerging] A systematic review identified ramipril (an ACEi) and losartan (an ARB) as showing potential benefit in slowing renal progression in Alport syndrome. Heterogeneity precluded quantitative synthesis, so no pooled or comparative effect estimate exists. Observational studies included in the review suggested that early intervention might delay dialysis. - PMID:40165927

[C | evidence supported] Retrospective studies found that ramipril delayed the onset of ESKD in Alport syndrome. The same review states that early initiation of RAAS blockade is very important. The time-to-kidney-failure evidence cited in these sources is ACEi-specific; no equivalent ARB time-to-kidney-failure data appear. - PMID:35547199

[C | evidence supported] Guidelines diverge on intensive targets. 2024 KDIGO suggests a systolic target below 120 mmHg for CKD. 2023 ESH recommends avoiding actively aiming for SBP below 120 or DBP below 70 mmHg. 2025 AHA/ACC sets a target below 130/80 and encourages SBP below 120 in high-risk patients. - PMID:41805831, PMID:42704524

[C | evidence supported] The evidence base for BP goals is more limited in stage 4-5 CKD. Intensive BP lowering is associated with electrolyte abnormalities and decreased eGFR that require careful laboratory monitoring. - PMID:30455322

[C | guideline supported] In CKD generally, guidelines broadly agree on dual-agent combination therapy, including RAS inhibitors in albuminuric CKD, with calcium-channel blockers or diuretics. Diuretic choice is guided by kidney function. For resistant hypertension, ESH positions chlorthalidone for eGFR below 30 and spironolactone for eGFR above 30. - PMID:38365947, PMID:42422469

[C | emerging] For ESRD there are no specific guidelines on antihypertensive therapy. One narrative review reports that treated ESRD patients have fewer cardiovascular events. It also notes that ARBs are not dialysed, ACE inhibitors are dialysable, and CCBs are non-dialysable and used second-line. Beta-blockers differ in dialysability. - PMID:42483492

[C | emerging] Achieving adequate 24-hour BP control appears to matter in CKD. Non-dipping combined with uncontrolled hypertension was associated with higher ESRD risk in pooled cohort data, and the Cochrane review calls for out-of-office monitoring in future trials. - PMID:42706969

[C | emerging] On maintenance haemodialysis, BP is intertwined with fluid shifts. Lung ultrasound has the strongest dialysis-specific evidence for detecting and tracking pulmonary congestion, which could inform volume and BP management. - PMID:42651080
[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of Alport syndrome management (four trials from six publications, plus two observational studies) found the following:
Ramipril and losartan, as well as bardoxolone methyl (a non-RAS agent), showed potential benefit in slowing renal disease progression.
Observational studies suggested early intervention might delay dialysis and improve life expectancy.
Heterogeneity prevented quantitative synthesis. - PMID:40165927

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews describe RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitors and ARBs) as the foundation of Alport treatment to delay kidney failure. They also note it does not target the underlying collagen IV defect and that its effectiveness is limited. - PMID:38927366, PMID:41243004

[C | evidence supported] Reviews and case series state that early and confirmed diagnosis of Alport syndrome enables effective intervention, including use of RAS inhibitors, and avoids unnecessary immunosuppression. - PMID:32712016, PMID:41555054

[C | evidence supported] RAS blockers can cause acute derangements in kidney function and hyperkalemia. One review advises caution with their use, particularly in advanced CKD, frailty, older age and cardiovascular disease. - PMID:28090762

[C | evidence supported] RAS blockers are described as first-line in CKD with micro- or macroalbuminuria (diabetic or not), with less relevant nephroprotection in non-proteinuric patients. International guidelines are summarised as strongly recommending ACEi/ARB with very high albuminuria. – of these statements is specific to G5 CKD. - PMID:28090762, PMID:37355779

[C | evidence supported] Dual RAS blockade produced greater antiproteinuric effect but no significant advantage on hard endpoints in large high-cardiovascular-risk trials, and is described as contraindicated in diabetic CKD. - PMID:28090762

[C | emerging] Modern potassium binders are described as able to preserve RAASi/MRA intensity in non-diabetic CKD with resistant hypertension, within a stepwise framework with structured monitoring. - PMID:42445746

[C | evidence supported] Hyperkalemia risk restricts broad use of the steroidal MRA spironolactone in moderate-to-advanced CKD. Finerenone's main safety concern is hyperkalemia. These data concern MRAs, not ACEi/ARB, but indicate that adding further potassium-raising agents is a recognised hazard in advanced CKD. - PMID:37355779, PMID:41293379

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews of CKD management list avoidance of potential nephrotoxins, with NSAIDs named as an example, plus drug-dose adjustment as components of optimal CKD care. No outcome data or guideline grading for this component are reported in the abstracts. - PMID:31573641, PMID:33708784

[C | emerging] A review on nephrotoxin stewardship asserts that implementing stewardship prevents drug-associated AKI and prevents progression or worsening of CKD. The abstract provides no supporting outcome data. - PMID:33752857

[C | evidence supported] In a propensity-matched prospective cohort of adult inpatients, high nephrotoxic medication and/or iodinated contrast exposure was associated with more in-hospital AKI (25.4% vs 15.8%). Vancomycin, iodinated contrast, piperacillin-tazobactam, antivirals and calcineurin/mTOR inhibitors contributed most to AKI-overlapping exposure days. This is an association with AKI, not with CKD progression or kidney failure. - PMID:42473493

[C | emerging] A primary-care review names antimicrobials, antihypertensives and NSAIDs as common offenders of drug-induced kidney injury, along with immunosuppressants, statins, PPIs and herbal supplements. When nephrotoxins cannot be avoided, it suggests hydration, avoiding concomitant nephrotoxins, and the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration. - PMID:33121637

[C | evidence supported] KDIGO-recommended kidney-protection strategies, which include avoiding radiocontrast and nephrotoxins when possible, have been studied in ICU AKI. Full adherence was associated with higher renal recovery at discharge in a multicentre cohort. A before-after bundle study found fewer moderate-to-severe AKI cases, but no significant change in overall AKI incidence. These are AKI settings, not stable advanced CKD. - PMID:42321935, PMID:42582794

[C | emerging] One review states that the degree of nephrotoxicity of contrast media remains inconclusive. This limits the evidentiary basis for contrast-specific avoidance recommendations. - PMID:34534999

[C | evidence supported] Drug dosing tables for adults with renal insufficiency exist that cover nephrotoxicity, adverse effects and adjustments for hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. Where specific data are lacking, recommendations rely on pharmacokinetics in normal subjects. - PMID:6356890

[C | evidence supported] In CKD, changes in protein binding, volume of distribution, kidney clearance and non-renal clearance require dose adjustment (shown here for antibiotics) to prevent toxicity. The adjustment strategy depends on drug pharmacodynamics, and newer dialysis technologies can remove more drug than originally reported. - PMID:30862698

[C | evidence supported] In CRRT, maintenance dosing depends on total clearance (residual renal, extracorporeal and non-renal), while loading doses depend mainly on volume of distribution. Therapeutic drug monitoring can guide adjustment where validated targets exist. - PMID:42942850

[C | evidence supported] For acute migraine therapy, NSAID use should be limited because of renal risk. Triptans may be used selectively with dose adjustment, and lasmiditan can be used in end-stage renal disease. - PMID:36709407

[C | evidence supported] Combining RAAS-blocking neuroendocrine inhibitors raises concern for hypotension, renal insufficiency and hyperkalemia, and close follow-up is advised when such agents are combined. - PMID:18060931

[C | evidence supported] In ESRD, ARBs are not affected by dialysis, whereas ACE inhibitors are dialyzable; calcium channel blockers are nondialyzable. The review notes a lack of specific guidelines for blood pressure therapy in ESRD. - PMID:42483492

[C | emerging] Apixaban dosing in kidney failure is unresolved. Pharmacokinetic data suggest 5 mg gives roughly 3-fold supratherapeutic exposure, but neither dose has been shown to reduce stroke versus no anticoagulation in this population. - PMID:42670022

[C | evidence supported] In CKD, traditional kidney-based dose limits for allopurinol or febuxostat may lead to undertreatment of gout. Allopurinol hypersensitivity risk factors, including HLA-B*5801 testing, are relevant. - PMID:40609855

[C | evidence supported] Updated 2020 recommendations for children, adolescents and young adults advise starting treatment at the time of diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome. This replaces the earlier approach of waiting for proteinuria. Treatment is based on RAAS interference to reduce proteinuria, intraglomerular pressure and fibrosis. - PMID:22461141, PMID:33159213
[C | evidence supported] ACE inhibition slows, but does not stop, progression to kidney failure in Alport syndrome. - PMID:27190345

[C | emerging] Emerging Alport-directed therapies have not yet reached standard care. The anti-miR-21 oligonucleotide lademirsen failed to show a clinically meaningful effect on kidney function decline in the phase 2 HERA trial. SGLT2 inhibitors and endothelin receptor antagonists remain under trial. - PMID:41853742, PMID:42783420

[C | evidence supported] ISRNM endorses the KDOQI guideline but suggests clinicians may use a streamlined target of 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day regardless of CKD cause, while aiming closer to 0.6 g/kg/day. - PMID:32737016

[C | evidence supported] Protein-energy wasting is described as a major predictor of morbidity and mortality in CKD even before dialysis. Adequate energy and protein record is described as the cornerstone of its management. - PMID:41683213

[C | evidence supported] For patients on dialysis, an international expert consensus advises nutritional screening and regular assessment for all patients. In those with PEW, oral nutritional supplements and/or intradialytic parenteral nutrition may help meet requirements. - PMID:42668650

[C | emerging] A 1984 narrative review of general chronic renal failure stated that dietary protein restriction protects residual renal function in rats and that dietary manipulation can slow loss of renal function in patients. This evidence is not specific to Alport syndrome. - PMID:6372657

[C | evidence supported] In advanced CKD, erythropoietin analogue (epoetin) therapy is described as remaining a key component of anaemia management. Biosimilar epoetins are approved, which is relevant to cost and access. - PMID:31477257

[C | evidence supported] Renal anaemia is attributed to insufficient renal erythropoietin production, iron metabolism disorders and chronic inflammation. The main drug pillars are ESAs, iron supplementation and HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors. - PMID:42713153

[C | evidence supported] In phase 3 trials, HIF-PHIs were non-inferior to conventional ESAs and superior to placebo for raising and maintaining haemoglobin, in both dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis CKD. Trials raised cardiovascular and thromboembolic safety concerns, particularly in non-dialysis-dependent patients. The US FDA has largely restricted approval to dialysis-dependent patients. - PMID:42610550
[C | emerging] The pooled residual-function benefit was described as mainly in PD; RCT evidence for residual function preservation in hemodialysis is not established by these sources. - PMID:28666408

[C | hypothesis] A narrative review notes that disease-progression pharmacotherapies are frequently associated with hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury at very low kidney function (<25% of normal). - PMID:40932799

[C | emerging] The cited prospective human trial data on ACE inhibitors come from children with early-stage CKD. – of the provided sources report human outcomes of ACE inhibitor initiation or continuation in late-steps (G4-G5) Alport-related CKD. - PMID:41272348
[C | evidence supported] Males with X-linked Alport syndrome are described as disproportionately severely affected, and management evidence specific to them remains limited. - PMID:40165927

[C | evidence supported] In the STOP-ACEi RCT (411 patients with advanced CKD), discontinuing RAAS inhibitors did not slow eGFR decline or reduce mortality at 3 years. Continuation showed only a numerical, non-definitive trend toward lower ESKD rates. - PMID:40207744

[C | evidence supported] Observational and meta-analytic data associate RAS inhibitor discontinuation in advanced CKD with higher major cardiovascular event and kidney failure/KRT risk. The meta-analysis found no mortality difference. These are associations, not proof of causation. - PMID:37214072, PMID:42851449

[C | evidence supported] Expert reviews conclude that RAASi continuation is supported in most CKD patients, including advanced disease, unless contraindicated. Use in advanced CKD remains debated because of hyperkalaemia, AKI and hypotension, and evidence in advanced CKD is described as limited. - PMID:40207744, PMID:41791738

[C | emerging] Reviews describe potassium binders and other adjuncts (for example SGLT2 inhibitors) as strategies that may allow RAASi use without discontinuation in high-risk patients. The cardiorenal benefit-versus-hyperkalaemia balance in CKD remains uncertain. - PMID:40207744, PMID:41611896

[C | emerging] The association between RASi and AKI is argued to be largely confounded by the underlying conditions (HFrEF, CKD, diabetes) rather than reflecting direct nephrotoxicity. - PMID:41921787

[C | evidence supported] A 2025 systematic review of Alport management found that ramipril and losartan, among others, showed potential benefit in slowing renal progression. Included observational studies indicated early intervention might delay dialysis and improve life expectancy. Heterogeneity precluded quantitative synthesis. - PMID:40165927

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews consistently describe early ACE inhibitor initiation as the focus of kidney therapy across all Alport genetic types. They note that RAAS blockade remains foundational to delaying kidney failure but does not target the underlying collagen IV defect. - PMID:37122389, PMID:41243004

[C | emerging] A randomized feasibility trial testing whether patiromer-enabled intensified RAASi (losartan/spironolactone) reduces albuminuria in CKD failed to recruit. Only 20 of the planned 98 participants completed, so no effect on albuminuria could be shown. The authors concluded that this design is unlikely to demonstrate renal benefit from binders. - PMID:39156169

[C | emerging] A review reports that in the BARACK-D RCT, adding spironolactone did not improve cardiovascular outcomes in moderate CKD, and its use was often limited by hyperkalemia. This illustrates that MRA use in CKD does not automatically translate into outcome benefit. - PMID:42162505

[C | hypothesis] Lower or discontinued RAASi dosing is associated with higher mortality in CKD, diabetes and HF. This association is the rationale for binder-enabled RAASi, but it is observational and does not prove that binder-enabled RAASi improves outcomes. - PMID:34150795

[C | evidence supported] Old-generation binders (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) lack randomized evidence for chronic use or for a RAASi-enabling effect, and carry fluid overload and colonic necrosis concerns. - PMID:37529653

[C | emerging] In PD trials, ARBs did not significantly change serum potassium compared with other antihypertensives, and one dialysis meta-analysis found no excess drug-related adverse events. - PMID:24953826, PMID:28666408

[C | evidence supported] Higher residual kidney function is associated with lower morbidity and mortality and better quality of life in both PD and HD. This is the rationale for trying to preserve it, but it is an association. - PMID:31630148, PMID:35819749

[C | emerging] The provided evidence on stopping versus continuing RAS inhibitors in advanced CKD is non-randomized. In a target trial emulation of the CKD-REIN cohort (eGFR <30, median eGFR 25), discontinuation was associated with about a two-fold higher adjusted 3-year risk of MACE and a higher risk of kidney replacement therapy initiation compared with continuation. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] In a multidatabase target trial emulation, discontinuing RAS inhibitors within 2 days of hospital-acquired AKI in long-term users was associated with lower 30-day all-cause mortality than continuation. This applies to an acute-injury context, not to stable advanced CKD. - PMID:40531580

[C | guideline supported] Recent nephrology guidance identifies advanced CKD and dialysis-treated kidney failure as populations where evidence for CKM pharmacotherapies, including RAS inhibitors, has important gaps. It also identifies glomerular disorders and younger individuals as such gaps. This is consistent with the absence of randomized stop-versus-continue data at very low eGFR in the provided sources. - PMID:42684397

[C | emerging] In RAAS inhibitor-treated patients with hyperkalemia, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate was associated with higher rates of maintaining RAAS inhibitor therapy. Effects on patient outcomes remain unproven. - PMID:42618199

[C | evidence supported] Expert clinical practice recommendations advise starting ACE inhibition at the time of diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome. They address early diagnosis and treatment, not advanced CKD or kidney failure. - PMID:33159213

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews state that ACE inhibitors delay progression to renal failure in Alport syndrome by reducing intraglomerular hypertension, proteinuria and fibrosis. They emphasise early initiation and early diagnosis. - PMID:25107927, PMID:32712016, PMID:37122389

[C | emerging] A retrospective multicentre cohort of Indian children with COL4A3-5 variants found that ACEI/ARB treatment had no significant impact on proteinuria or CKD progression at follow-up. - PMID:42955332

[C | hypothesis] A mechanistic review distinguishes proteinuria from podocyte dysfunction, which may be partially modifiable, from proteinuria associated with podocyte loss and glomerulosclerosis, which is less likely to be reversible. This implies that anti-proteinuric therapies may have less disease-modifying effect in advanced disease. - PMID:42949772

[C | evidence supported] The European Alport Registry prospective analysis cannot inform an ARB-versus-ACEi comparison. Its cohort was heterozygous carriers, not hemizygous males, almost all treated patients received an ACEi, and only one received an ARB. - PMID:27402170

[C | evidence supported] A 2025 systematic review identified ramipril (ACEi) and losartan (ARB) as showing potential benefit in slowing Alport kidney disease progression. Heterogeneity precluded pooled analysis, and no stratified ACEi-versus-ARB time-to-kidney-failure result is reported in the abstract. - PMID:40165927
[C | evidence supported] Expert consensus treats ACEi and ARB together as the mainstay of current Alport therapy, without distinguishing their outcomes. - PMID:31044288

[C | emerging] An adult narrative review states that RAAS inhibition should not be discontinued in advanced CKD. It also states that an initial eGFR fall of no more than 30% after starting treatment should be seen as a marker of long-term renoprotective success, not a reason to stop. - PMID:39503219

[C | emerging] A paediatric review notes that the role of RAAS inhibitors in advanced CKD remains controversial. Clinicians may stop them because of worsening kidney function, hyperkalaemia and hypotension, but current data suggest stopping may lead to faster kidney function decline. - PMID:33057769

[C | evidence supported] Patients with CKD are at heightened risk of hyperkalaemia, which can be fatal if untreated. Sources emphasise electrolyte monitoring when using RAAS inhibition. One review notes that reduced renal function raises hyperkalaemia risk and limits the use of MR antagonists. - PMID:41189867, PMID:42110960, PMID:42733634

[C | evidence supported] Interdialytic home BP and ambulatory BP monitoring are reported to be prognostically more informative than in-centre predialysis BP in dialysis patients. Expert opinion favours focusing on out-of-dialysis-unit BPs. - PMID:28938954, PMID:30422343, PMID:41982586

[C | evidence supported] No dialysis-specific BP target is established. No adequately designed trial comparing BP targets in haemodialysis exists, so firm target recommendations are not possible. - PMID:28938954, PMID:30084190, PMID:30422343, PMID:32278617

[C | emerging] In dialysis, observational data show low BP associated with worse outcomes (a U-shaped relationship). This is considered likely due to confounding, since the relationship appears more linear in patients with fewer cardiovascular comorbidities and longer survival. - PMID:30422343, PMID:41982586

[C | evidence supported] Meta-analyses of RCTs are cited as showing that deliberate BP lowering improves clinical outcomes in haemodialysis. Sodium and volume control are first-line considerations: dietary sodium restriction, individualised dialysate sodium, dry-weight optimisation and sufficient dialysis duration. Antihypertensive drugs are the next step. - PMID:30084190

[C | emerging] Volume-related measures are associated with BP and cardiovascular risk in dialysis. Higher ABPM-derived diastolic BP variability and interdialytic weight gain were associated with cardiovascular events in a retrospective cohort. Target-weight optimisation guided by modified VExUS ultrasound was associated with lower systolic BP in a small prospective study. - PMID:41820019, PMID:42879334

[C | evidence supported] Intradialytic BP phenotypes are distinct issues. Intradialytic hypertension affects about 10-15% of haemodialysis patients and raises cardiovascular risk. In intradialytic hypotension, the stated concern is organ hypoperfusion, with objective volume assessment as the first step. - PMID:39585515, PMID:42975009

[C | evidence supported] A meta-analysis of four studies in advanced CKD found that RAS inhibitor discontinuation was associated with more cardiovascular events (HR 1.38) and more ESKD (HR 1.29) than continuation. It found no significant difference in all-cause mortality. - PMID:37214072

[C | evidence supported] RAS inhibitors are often stopped in advanced CKD to limit adverse effects or to delay kidney replacement therapy. In the emulation cohort, adverse drug reaction events cluster just before discontinuation. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] Hyperkalaemia-mitigation strategies, including potassium binders, are proposed as a way to avoid discontinuing RAAS inhibitors in CKD. Whether the benefits outweigh hyperkalaemia risk remains uncertain. - PMID:41611896

[C | evidence supported] Small eGFR declines after starting guideline-directed heart-failure therapies, including RAAS inhibitors, are generally haemodynamic. They are not associated with poor outcomes and generally do not require discontinuation. Evidence in advanced CKD is limited. - PMID:41791738, PMID:41793402

[C | guideline supported] Guidance and reviews identify evidence gaps for advanced CKD, dialysis, younger individuals and nonmetabolic (glomerular) kidney diseases. All of these apply to this patient. - PMID:42397326, PMID:42684397

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews state that RAAS blockade (ACE inhibitor and/or ARB) has a well-established renoprotective effect in Alport syndrome and can significantly delay the onset of renal replacement therapy and ESKD. The underlying registry or cohort numbers, and any stratification by start stage, are not given in the abstract. - PMID:22903660, PMID:38745975

[C | evidence supported] Expert clinical practice recommendations (2020 update) advise starting ACE inhibition at the time of diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome. This is a shift from the 2013 approach of waiting for overt proteinuria or microalbuminuria, and implies that earlier treatment is considered more beneficial. - PMID:33159213

[C | evidence supported] A review states that the availability of effective intervention makes early diagnosis of Alport syndrome crucial. This is consistent with treatment benefit depending on early initiation, but gives no quantification for late starts. - PMID:32712016

[C | evidence supported] The clinical course and prognosis of Alport syndrome vary widely and are influenced by sex, inheritance mode, affected gene, variant type and genetic modifiers. Interpreting any treatment-timing effect therefore depends on genotype context. - PMID:39004457

[C | evidence supported] In the STOP-ACEi randomized trial (advanced CKD), stopping RAAS inhibition did not slow eGFR decline or reduce mortality after 3 years. Continuing was associated only with a numerical (not demonstrated) trend toward lower ESKD rates. A difference in time to kidney replacement therapy was therefore not established either way. - PMID:40207744

[C | evidence supported] A review concludes that current evidence supports continuing RAASi in most CKD patients, including those with advanced disease, unless contraindicated. It also notes that use in advanced CKD is debated because of hyperkalaemia, AKI and hypotension risks. - PMID:40207744

[C | evidence supported] In a cross-sectional cohort of non-dialysis CKD with measured GFR, RAASi use was independently associated with hyperkalaemia, defined as potassium ≥5.0 mmol/L or binder use. The GFR-hyperkalaemia association was amplified in RAASi users, and prevalence reached 21% in stages 4-5. Lower bicarbonate and higher albuminuria were also associated. - PMID:42664185

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews recommend treating chronic hyperkalaemia before reducing or stopping RAASi, because interruption may increase adverse cardiovascular and renal outcomes. They highlight newer potassium binders and SGLT2 inhibitors as adjuncts that may allow safer RAASi use, with potassium monitored before and throughout treatment. - PMID:37775712, PMID:40207744
[C | evidence supported] Combination ACEi/ARB therapy provides no additional benefit and increases adverse events, including hyperkalaemia and hypotension. - PMID:40207744

[D | hypothesis] Ramipril label: baseline renal function should be established before starting. Usual regimens apply only when estimated creatinine clearance is above 40 mL/min, with a reduced starting dose in renal impairment. Contraindications include prior ACEi-associated or hereditary/idiopathic angioedema and combination with a neprilysin inhibitor. - DB:f2db68e8c28ad4a2

[D | hypothesis] The losartan FDA label warns that drugs inhibiting the renin-angiotensin system can cause changes in renal function, including acute renal failure. Patients with CKD or volume depletion may be at particular risk. Losartan is contraindicated with aliskiren in diabetes. - DB:dede7cc9a08afab5

[D | emerging] A narrative review of adult ICU acute kidney injury lists nephrotoxin stewardship among current critical care kidney practices, alongside fluid stewardship and recovery planning. - PMID:42375913

[D | emerging] A narrative review of myeloma-related renal dysfunction lists hydration, avoidance of nephrotoxins and electrolyte monitoring as essential care components. It also emphasises pharmacist roles in preventing nephrotoxic exposure and adjusting regimens. - PMID:42824767

[D | hypothesis] Digital (mHealth) nutrition interventions showed no significant effects on biochemical outcomes or interdialytic weight gain in dialysis patients. Observational data link ultra-processed food record with CKD progression, but causality is not established. - PMID:42797038, PMID:42942928

[D | hypothesis] In controlled CKD trials, targeting higher Hb increased death, cardiovascular events and stroke. The label warns that no Hb target or dosing strategy has been shown free of these risks and advises the lowest dose sufficient to reduce transfusions. - DB:cd2336d47c9cd2c2

[D | hypothesis] Label initiation criteria: for adults on dialysis, initiate at Hb <10 g/dL. For adults not on dialysis, consider only when Hb <10 g/dL and either the rate of decline suggests a transfusion is likely and/or reducing alloimmunisation or other transfusion risks is a goal. The patient's current Hb of 10.4 g/dL is above this threshold. - DB:cd2336d47c9cd2c2

[D | hypothesis] The FDA label for iron sucrose lists known hypersensitivity as a contraindication. Its dosage sections cover adults with haemodialysis-dependent, peritoneal-dialysis-dependent and non-dialysis-dependent CKD. - DB:add28e41033d2e42

[D | hypothesis] The patiromer label states that no special dose adjustment is needed in renal impairment, and 93% of treated trial patients had CKD. The only stated contraindication is hypersensitivity. The label excerpt does not specifically address eGFR below 15 or dialysis. - DB:03992a7a8bcaca16

[D | emerging] Post-transplant anti-GBM disease is reported more often with COL4A5 gene deletions than with point mutations. The patient's variant is a missense (Gly substitution) VUS, so his risk may be lower than with deletions but is not excluded. - PMID:14717941

[D | emerging] After a first graft is lost to anti-GBM nephritis, recurrence with accelerated rejection on retransplantation has been reported repeatedly. Anti-T-cell therapy, plasma exchange and mycophenolate did not prevent graft loss in the described cases. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[D | hypothesis] Standard anti-GBM ELISA can be negative in Alport post-transplant anti-GBM disease. Western blotting against alpha5(IV) NC1 was more sensitive and specific. An isolated serological anti-GBM response without clinical nephritis is also described. - PMID:14717941, PMID:42390934

[D | evidence supported] Transplantation outcomes in Alport syndrome are described as generally favourable when guided by molecular confirmation and careful donor evaluation. In a three-patient series, the two X-linked recipients had a COVID-19-associated arterial thrombosis with graft loss and late antibody-mediated rejection at six years. - PMID:42076904

[D | emerging] Indirect evidence comes from 93 donor-recipient pairs. Kidneys from donors with biopsy-proven thin basement membrane disease had graft function and survival equivalent to kidneys from hematuric donors with normal histology over a median of 3 years. The authors call for genetically stratified studies. - PMID:42922936

[D | emerging] Alport-specific evidence is limited and the two reviews differ. A 2025 review lists SGLT2 inhibitors among available novel treatments for persistent albuminuria despite RAAS blockade. A 2022 review notes only a handful of Alport patients in DAPA-CKD and says conclusions cannot be extrapolated. - PMID:35547199, PMID:39840589

[D | emerging] In Alport syndrome, RAAS blockade is described as the foundation of treatment to delay kidney failure. Sparsentan (dual endothelin/angiotensin receptor inhibition) is described only as an investigational therapy being tested in Phase II trials; no Alport-specific efficacy outcomes are reported in the provided sources. - PMID:35547199, PMID:41243004

[D | emerging] In Alport syndrome, RAAS blockade is the foundation of treatment. Atrasentan is only being tested in Phase II trials, and the sources report no patient-important outcome data for atrasentan in Alport syndrome. - PMID:35547199, PMID:41243004

[D | hypothesis] In Col4a3-deficient mice (an Alport model) with established nephropathy, late-onset ramipril monotherapy attenuated CKD and prolonged survival by about 2 weeks. Adding empagliflozin and finerenone extended survival further. - PMID:37428955

[D | hypothesis] No provided source reports ACE inhibitor effects on serum potassium in people near or on dialysis. The only related datapoint is a 4-patient case series of sacubitril/valsartan in HFrEF patients on hemodialysis, in which potassium was reported as stable without severe hyperkalemia. - PMID:42784016

[D | hypothesis] Discontinuation in advanced CKD is often driven by adverse effects such as hyperkalaemia. A narrative review proposes that potassium binders and other strategies could avoid the need to stop RAAS inhibitors, but this has not been tested on outcomes in the sources. - PMID:41611896, PMID:42851449

[D | hypothesis] In Col4a3-deficient mice with established nephropathy, late-onset ramipril monotherapy attenuated CKD and prolonged survival by about 2 weeks. Ramipril plus empagliflozin had a similar effect, and adding finerenone extended survival further. An earlier review of mouse studies also reports ACE inhibitors as effective in Alport mice. - PMID:25374816, PMID:37428955

[D | hypothesis] Electrolyte monitoring is emphasised as key when using RAAS blockade. A single reported adult with proteinuric CKD had albuminuria reduction and kidney function stabilisation without clinically significant hyperkalemia. - PMID:41189867

[D | hypothesis] A small case series reports that kidney transplantation is effective in Alport syndrome when guided by molecular confirmation and careful donor evaluation. It also notes vascular events and late antibody-mediated rejection in X-linked cases. - PMID:42076904

[D | hypothesis] Ketoanalogue-supplemented low-protein diets are described as delaying CKD progression in a narrative review. In a Markov cost-utility model for stage 4+ CKD, they modelled gains in survival and delayed dialysis versus a standard low-protein diet. - PMID:40790782, PMID:41978192

[D | hypothesis] In an X-linked Alport (Col4a5-deficient) mouse model, an animal-protein, high-phosphate Western-type diet worsened CKD-MBD components compared with a vegetable-protein, lower-phosphate diet. Reported changes were higher PTH and FGF23, reduced renal klotho and reduced cardiac mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. - PMID:39896481, PMID:41481362

[D | hypothesis] In the same Alport mouse model, the high-phosphate Western diet did not induce vascular calcification, although the model is described as resistant to vascular calcification. - PMID:39896481, PMID:41481362

[D | emerging] In managing patients with a failing kidney graft, strategies to prevent HLA sensitisation and increase retransplant rates are described as emerging priorities. This indicates sensitisation is a recognised transplant-access concern, but the source does not link it to transfusion or ESA use. - PMID:36294429

[D | hypothesis] In a mouse Alport model, adding spironolactone to ramipril reduced proteinuria and fibrosis but did not further extend survival, possibly because of hyperkalemia. This is animal data only and a hypothesis-level safety signal for combined RAAS blockade. - PMID:34209341

[D | hypothesis] In a preclinical randomised trial in Col4a3-deficient mice with established Alport nephropathy, late-onset ramipril monotherapy prolonged survival by about 2 weeks. The mice already had elevated creatinine, albuminuria and fibrosis. - PMID:37428955

[D | hypothesis] In autosomal recessive Alport syndrome, patients with one or two missense variants responded better to RAAS inhibition than those with non-missense variants. Whether this applies to hemizygous COL4A5 missense (glycine-substitution) variants in X-linked disease is untested in these sources. - PMID:33772369

[D | hypothesis] No direct trial evidence in the provided sources shows that RAS inhibitors preserve RKF in haemodialysis. RAAS blockade is listed only as a proposed strategy in narrative reviews, and HD guidelines rarely give operational RKF guidance. - PMID:31630148, PMID:42878663

[D | emerging] In a small single-centre observational study, APD was associated with faster RKF decline than CAPD in the first 6 months. The RAS-inhibitor RKF evidence above comes mainly from CAPD. - PMID:42802590

[D | hypothesis] A small retrospective cohort reported improved kidney function over about 4 years after elective withdrawal of long-term RAAS blockade, without increased cardiovascular mortality. This was in CKD patients presenting with otherwise unexplained progressive AKI. - PMID:36447726

[E | hypothesis] The sparsentan trial and real-world populations in the sources had moderately reduced kidney function at most (largest PROTECT group CKD 3B; Spanish real-world median eGFR 44). No source provides efficacy or safety data at CKD G5 or eGFR <15. - PMID:37180506, PMID:42746507

[E | hypothesis] The provided evidence does not support atrasentan use at this level of kidney function. SONAR excluded eGFR <25 and counted eGFR <15 as a kidney-failure outcome, and the patient's eGFR is already 6.2. - PMID:39661119

[E | hypothesis] All finerenone trials in the sources enrolled patients with eGFR of at least 25 mL/min/1.73 m2. No source provides efficacy or safety data at eGFR below 25 or on dialysis, which includes the patient's eGFR of 6.2. - PMID:34449181, PMID:38858818, PMID:41780000

[E | hypothesis] The LIFT trial is a double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT protocol of SZC to support up-titration of RAASi in patients with advanced CKD and heart failure. Its primary outcome is the proportion reaching maximum RAASi dose while normokalaemic. Results are not available in the sources. - PMID:34229607

[E | hypothesis] The KDOQI 2020 nutrition guideline explicitly covers dialysis patients and includes dietary protein and energy record as a core area. However, none of the provided abstracts states the numeric protein target for patients on maintenance hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, so the pre- versus post-dialysis comparison cannot be made from these sources. - PMID:32829751, PMID:33158799
