blocks.text: Verified research findings (87)

items: [A | evidence supported] Across randomized trials in CKD, combined RAAS blockade (dual therapy vs monotherapy) was associated with higher serum potassium and higher rates of hyperkalaemia and hypotension. - PMID:23382494, PMID:34477114

[A | guideline supported] An international guideline (ERKNet/ERA/ESPN 2024), based on a systematic literature review and graded consensus, states that early renin-angiotensin system blockade is the standard of care for COL4A3/4/5 glomerulopathy including Alport syndrome. SGLT2 inhibitors may be added in adults with proteinuria and CKD. - PMID:39673454

[A | evidence supported] In RCTs pooled in a meta-analysis of diabetic kidney disease, ACEi + ARB dual therapy was associated with more hyperkalaemia and AKI than ACEi or ARB monotherapy. - PMID:37309038

[A | evidence supported] In a broad CKD meta-analysis of 72 RCTs, dual RAAS blockade reduced albuminuria and BP, but at the cost of lower GFR, higher potassium, more hyperkalaemia and more hypotension. It did not improve hard outcomes. - PMID:34477114

[B | evidence supported] Trial-level modelling estimates that ACEi/ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor substantially reduces the composite of creatinine doubling, kidney failure or death versus no treatment, in albuminuric CKD without diabetes. - PMID:36414316

[B | evidence supported] In an individual patient-level meta-analysis of 38 cohorts, UACR was more strongly associated with kidney failure than UPCR. The authors conclude UACR is preferred for diagnosing and risk-stratifying CKD. This is a prognostic and staging test, not a test that discriminates between aetiologies. - PMID:41183334

[B | evidence supported] Combined RAAS blockade reduced albuminuria/proteinuria and blood pressure. However, neither meta-analysis found improvement in hard outcomes (doubling of serum creatinine, acute kidney injury, end-stage renal disease, hospitalization or mortality) versus monotherapy. - PMID:23382494, PMID:34477114

[B | evidence supported] The 2013 meta-analysis found a net decrease in GFR with combined blockade. A narrative review states that combining ACEi and ARB brought no further benefit while increasing the risk of hyperkalaemia, hypotension and acute renal failure, and argues clinical use should be limited to strictly selected patients. - PMID:23382494, PMID:28471687

[B | evidence supported] In a target trial emulation (CKD-REIN cohort, eGFR <30, n=1434), discontinuing RAS inhibitors was associated with about twice the 3-year risk of major cardiovascular events and a 34% higher risk of KRT initiation. The authors conclude that continued use with close monitoring is favoured. - PMID:42851449

[B | evidence supported] The EARLY PRO-TECT randomized controlled trial of ramipril vs placebo in children with early-stage Alport syndrome was under-enrolled and not formally positive. It is described as providing strong supportive evidence for long-term safety and for slowing progression of albuminuria and eGFR decline. - PMID:32444091

[B | evidence supported] Excess acute kidney injury with ACEi + ARB versus monotherapy was reported in two meta-analyses of RCTs. The abstract of the DKD meta-analysis gives a confidence interval (1.23-1.39) that does not contain its point estimate (RR 1.48), suggesting a reporting error. - PMID:37309038, PMID:41798419

[B | evidence supported] In the only randomized trial provided (STOP-ACEi; advanced, progressive CKD, eGFR below 30), stopping RAS inhibitors did not significantly change eGFR at 3 years. The ESKD or kidney-replacement endpoint was numerically more frequent after stopping, but this did not reach significance. Cardiovascular events and deaths were similar between groups. - PMID:36326117

[B | evidence supported] A meta-analysis of 9 RCTs in CKD stage 4-5 associated RAAS blockade with reduced progression to ESKD, with no effect on all-cause mortality or MACE. It pooled use vs non-use, initiation, and discontinuation-vs-continuation strategies. - PMID:38458564

[B | evidence supported] In the OPAL-HK RCT, patiromer lowered serum potassium in CKD patients on RAAS inhibitors with hyperkalaemia. In the randomized withdrawal phase it reduced hyperkalaemia recurrence versus placebo while RAASi continued. - PMID:25415805

[B | evidence supported] In the prespecified subgroup aged 65 years or older from OPAL-HK, patiromer similarly reduced recurrent hyperkalaemia versus placebo in CKD patients taking RAASi. - PMID:29180023

[B | evidence supported] A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (1697 patients) found SZC reduced serum potassium versus placebo. Efficacy was consistent in studies with more than 50% CKD or RAASi-using patients. - PMID:33459923

[B | evidence supported] Binder-specific adverse effects reported: constipation, hypokalaemia and low magnesium with patiromer, and higher oedema risk with SZC versus placebo. - PMID:25415805, PMID:29180023, PMID:33459923

[B | evidence supported] In a target trial emulation from a prospective cohort, the CKD-Renal Epidemiology and Information Network (CKD-REIN), 1434 patients with eGFR <30 were treated with RAS inhibitors. Discontinuing, compared with continuing, was associated with a 3-year adjusted relative risk of 2.02 for major cardiovascular events and 1.34 for starting kidney replacement therapy. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] In a small observational paediatric cohort with proteinuric chronic nephropathies and largely preserved kidney function, ramipril plus losartan up-titrated to maximum tolerated doses was associated with proteinuria remission in a subset. Hyperkalaemia occurred in 2 of 20 children. - PMID:27704256

[C | evidence supported] Patients with advanced renal insufficiency were excluded from the RAS-inhibitor renoprotection trials because of acute renal failure and hyperkalaemia risk. A post hoc REIN analysis suggested single-agent RAS inhibition was safe and slowed GFR decline only in patients with baseline GFR 10-30 mL/min/1.73m2. - PMID:12243375
[C | hypothesis] ACE inhibitors and ARBs are described as having considerably overlapping benefits and side effects, with ARBs possibly having a lower incidence of hyperkalaemia. - PMID:14871059

[C | emerging] The same source states, as background, that RAAS inhibitors are the most studied treatment for Alport syndrome, with benefits for renal function and survival in animals and humans. - PMID:40499560
[C | emerging] In a 24-week RCT, adding dapagliflozin to ramipril reduced albumin excretion rate by 43.5% versus ramipril alone. Participants had type 2 diabetes and preserved eGFR. - PMID:36247425

[C | emerging] In a small mechanistic crossover RCT in type 1 diabetes, adding empagliflozin to ramipril lowered measured GFR by about 8 mL/min/1.73m2 versus placebo-ramipril. The combination also produced additive clinic blood-pressure lowering. The authors interpreted these as a protective haemodynamic profile (lower intraglomerular pressure). - PMID:35862082

[C | emerging] A narrative review of type 2 diabetes-associated albuminuric CKD states that a modest early eGFR decline after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor usually reflects a functional haemodynamic response rather than drug-related injury. - PMID:42741732

[C | emerging] The same review suggests simultaneous initiation of kidney-protective combinations is most appropriate with stable eGFR, normal or low-normal potassium and reliable monitoring access. It describes hyperkalaemia management as baseline risk stratification plus early potassium surveillance; this guidance is written for finerenone, not ramipril. - PMID:42741732

[C | evidence supported] Serum cystatin C is described as an accurate CKD biomarker. It is most useful when creatinine is an inadequate marker of GFR or when a false-positive low creatinine-based eGFR is suspected. - PMID:29431364, PMID:32450046

[C | evidence supported] Standard CKD detection uses serum creatinine, urine albumin/creatinine ratio and urinalysis. After diagnosis, evaluation should focus on the specific type of kidney disease and on stage-related complications. - PMID:22085668, PMID:29431364
[C | evidence supported] Nephrology consultation is indicated for eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, significant proteinuria, or evidence of rapid loss of kidney function. - PMID:22085668, PMID:29431364

[C | evidence supported] Point-of-care blood gas potassium may overestimate serum potassium. It should be confirmed with a laboratory sample unless urgent treatment is needed. This helps separate a measurement artefact from true hyperkalaemia. - PMID:42935704

[C | evidence supported] An ECG identifies cardiac effects of hyperkalaemia, and ECG changes make cardiac protection the immediate priority. This sets urgency rather than discriminating the cause. - PMID:42935704

[C | evidence supported] Expert consensus (KDIGO Controversies Conference) notes that potassium disorders are common in kidney disease, particularly with tubular disorders and low GFR. It proposes a hypokalaemia diagnostic algorithm that gives priority to clinical context in determining cause. - PMID:31706619

[C | evidence supported] Assessing reversible triggers is part of the evaluation, including drugs that can raise potassium such as RAAS inhibitors. Concurrent metabolic acidosis is identified as a context that changes management. - PMID:42935704

[C | emerging] The 2021 meta-analysis concluded that ACEI+ARB was the better dual combination than ACEI or ARB plus a renin inhibitor or MRA. It suggested that individualized management and potassium binders may expand use despite higher hyperkalaemia and hypotension. - PMID:34477114
[C | evidence supported] In moderate-to-advanced CKD, hyperkalaemia risk is described as limiting the use of spironolactone (an aldosterone antagonist added on top of RAS blockade). - PMID:37355779

[C | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of 4 studies in advanced CKD, discontinuing RAS inhibitors was associated with more cardiovascular events and more ESKD than continuing them. All-cause mortality did not differ significantly. - PMID:37214072

[C | emerging] Adverse drug reaction events were rare overall but clustered in the 3 months before RAS inhibitor discontinuation. This suggests discontinuation is often triggered by adverse effects, which may confound the comparison. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] RAAS inhibitors increase hyperkalaemia risk. A review proposes potassium binders and kidney-protective drugs as ways to avoid stopping them, while stating that the optimal potassium range and the balance against hyperkalaemia in CKD remain uncertain. - PMID:41611896

[C | emerging] The KDIGO controversies conference states that evidence for RAAS inhibitors and related agents in advanced CKD remains limited. It also states that small declines in kidney function after starting guideline-directed HF therapies generally do not require discontinuation. - PMID:41791738, PMID:41793402

[C | evidence supported] In a registry study of 101 patients with autosomal recessive Alport syndrome, untreated patients reached CKD5 at a median age of 24 years. RAAS inhibition delayed CKD5 onset to a median age of 35 years in those who started with already impaired kidney function. No treated patients with microalbuminuria progressed to CKD5, and patients with missense variants responded better. - PMID:33772369

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review (four trials, two observational studies) found that ramipril, losartan and bardoxolone methyl showed potential benefit in slowing renal progression in Alport syndrome. Observational data suggested early intervention may delay dialysis. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis. - PMID:40165927

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews describe RAAS blockade/early ACE inhibition as the foundation of treatment across Alport types. They note that it does not target the underlying collagen IV defect, and that males with X-linked Alport syndrome have more severe disease. - PMID:37122389, PMID:41243004

[C | evidence supported] Reviews characterise ACEi + ARB dual blockade as not recommended or to be used with caution, because it adds harm without benefit. – of the provided sources describes it as a formal contraindication. - PMID:28471687, PMID:33550292, PMID:41798419

[C | emerging] In an observational target-trial emulation of patients with eGFR below 30 on RAS inhibitors, stopping was associated with roughly double the 3-year risk of major cardiovascular events. It was also associated with a 34% higher relative risk of starting kidney replacement therapy, compared with continuing. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] During hospital-acquired acute kidney injury in long-term RAS inhibitor users, stopping the RAS inhibitor within 2 days was associated with lower all-cause mortality. This applies to the acute-injury setting, not to stable advanced CKD. - PMID:40531580

[C | evidence supported] In RAS-inhibitor-treated patients with high potassium, the potassium binder sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) was associated with better maintenance and up-titration of RAS inhibitors. Benefit for cardiovascular or kidney outcomes has not been shown. - PMID:42618199

[C | evidence supported] Clinical practice recommendations (2020 update) advise starting ACE inhibition at the time of diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome, rather than waiting for overt proteinuria. The emphasis is on early initiation, not on advanced CKD. - PMID:33159213

[C | evidence supported] Reviews describe RAAS blockade as the foundation of Alport treatment to delay kidney failure. They also stress that early diagnosis matters because effective intervention is available. This implies benefit is concentrated in earlier disease. - PMID:32712016, PMID:41243004

[C | hypothesis] A mechanistic review distinguishes two components of Alport proteinuria. Podocyte dysfunction with foot-process effacement may be partially modifiable. Proteinuria from podocyte loss and glomerulosclerosis is less likely to be reversible. This suggests that the potential to modify disease declines as disease advances. - PMID:42949772

[C | emerging] In a retrospective multicentre cohort of 108 Indian children with COL4A variants (60 XLAS), ACEI use (68.5%) showed no significant impact on proteinuria or CKD at 5-year follow-up. - PMID:42955332

[C | evidence supported] The patient's XLAS diagnosis relies on a clinical and family-history picture plus a COL4A5 VUS. A precision-nephrology review states that VUS should not independently determine treatment. - PMID:42792963

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews report that dual RAAS blockade is associated with a higher risk of hyperkalaemia. They also report that it has not been shown to be superior on validated renal end points (doubling of creatinine, time to dialysis, death) in CKD. - PMID:19737451, PMID:20664560

[C | evidence supported] RAAS antagonists have dose-limiting adverse effects, namely acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and hypotension. Patients with combined CKD and heart failure are at the greatest risk of these events, and several dual-blockade trials failed to improve clinical outcomes. - PMID:27278080

[C | evidence supported] The ACEi/ARB combination is described as producing BP reductions not significantly greater than either drug alone, while being frequently associated with more side effects. - PMID:20467589

[C | evidence supported] RAAS blockade with ACE inhibitors or ARBs is described as the standard, foundational therapy to delay progression toward kidney failure in Alport syndrome. The underlying evidence is predominantly from earlier-stage disease, and the only systematic review could not pool results because of heterogeneity. - PMID:26995302, PMID:40165927, PMID:41243004

[C | evidence supported] Expert recommendations favour early initiation: at diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome. Observational data suggest that early intervention may delay dialysis. This timing emphasis implies the evidence base is strongest well before advanced CKD. - PMID:33159213, PMID:40165927

[C | emerging] Dual ACEi plus ARB blockade in Alport syndrome is reported only as having 'mixed success'. Renin inhibitors and aldosterone blockade are described as used with positive results. No quantitative or advanced-CKD data are provided. - PMID:26995302

[C | hypothesis] Late-stage proteinuria in Alport syndrome reflects podocyte loss and glomerulosclerosis, which is described as less likely to be reversible. Therapeutic strategy is said to depend on which mechanisms predominate at each disease stage. This offers a mechanistic rationale, not tested evidence, for why haemodynamic or RAAS-directed benefit may be smaller in advanced disease. - PMID:40938675, PMID:42949772
[C | emerging] SGLT2 inhibitors are noted as an add-on option for persistent albuminuria despite RAAS blockade in Alport syndrome. Their use at very low eGFR is not addressed. - PMID:39840589

[C | evidence supported] A multicentre RCT (STOP-ACEi, n=411, advanced CKD) found that discontinuing RAS inhibitors did not slow eGFR decline or reduce mortality over 3 years. Continuation showed a numerical (non-significant) trend toward fewer ESKD events. - PMID:40207744

[C | evidence supported] A 2025 review concludes that current evidence supports RAS inhibitor continuation in most CKD patients, including those with advanced disease, unless contraindicated. It notes that use at eGFR <30 is debated because of hyperkalaemia, AKI and hypotension risks. - PMID:40207744
[C | evidence supported] Dual ACEi/ARB therapy adds no benefit and increases hyperkalaemia and hypotension. - PMID:40207744

[C | emerging] Potassium binders and SGLT2 inhibitors are proposed as adjuncts that may enable safer RAS inhibitor use in high-risk patients. This is a suggestion, not proven by the cited randomized discontinuation data. - PMID:40207744

[C | evidence supported] Before STOP-ACEi, RCTs on initiating or maintaining RAS blockers in advanced CKD were described as scarce and excluding normoalbuminuric patients. Fear of hyperkalaemia drives frequent discontinuation at stages 4-5. - PMID:33654237

[C | evidence supported] Reviews describe RAAS blockade, specifically ACE inhibitors (ARB if ACEi not tolerated), as the foundation of kidney treatment in Alport syndrome. ACE inhibition is reported to slow progression and delay kidney failure by years. It does not target the underlying collagen IV defect. - PMID:38745975, PMID:41243004

[C | evidence supported] Benefit of ACE inhibition is framed around early or very early initiation. No source reports benefit of initiating ACE inhibition at advanced CKD or near kidney failure in humans. - PMID:36553470, PMID:37122389

[C | evidence supported] Males with X-linked Alport syndrome are described as having more severe disease. Missense variants are generally associated with milder, more protracted kidney involvement. This patient's very rapid decline with a Gly missense VUS does not match the typical missense pattern described. - PMID:37122389

[C | emerging] A small randomized crossover trial in advanced CKD on RAAS inhibition found hyperkalaemia occurring during a potassium-enriched diet was managed with SZC. Both the diet and RAAS inhibition were continued. - PMID:42636918

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews state that potassium binders allow continuation or preservation of RAASi/MRA therapy. One review also states that risk increases when RAASi is discontinued after hyperkalaemia. - PMID:37583425, PMID:40841869, PMID:41953780

[C | evidence supported] A meta-analysis of four studies in advanced CKD found RAS inhibitor discontinuation associated with significantly more cardiovascular events and more ESKD than continuation. There was no significant difference in all-cause mortality. - PMID:37214072

[C | evidence supported] Confounding by indication is a key methodological concern in discontinuation studies. In the emulation cohort, adverse drug reactions clustered in the 3 months before discontinuation, although they were few in absolute number. - PMID:42851449

[C | emerging] Evidence for continuing RAS inhibitors and other kidney-protective drugs is weaker in CKD G5 than in G4. One review states that G5 decisions remain individualized and extrapolative, and that landmark trials enrolled participants down to eGFR thresholds of about 20-30. Other sources note that evidence in advanced CKD is limited and that these drugs are frequently difficult to use there. - PMID:40395996, PMID:41793402, PMID:42890508

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews state that routine discontinuation of RAS blockade in advanced CKD does not improve kidney function and may increase cardiorenal risk. They describe hyperkalaemia mitigation strategies, including potassium binders, as a way to avoid discontinuing RAAS inhibitors. - PMID:41611896, PMID:42445746, PMID:42521294

[D | hypothesis] In FAERS spontaneous reports for nine ACE inhibitors (including lisinopril and ramipril), the most commonly reported adverse events were angioedema, cough, hypotension and acute kidney injury. Because FAERS lacks denominators, these are reporting patterns and not incidence or risk estimates. The analysis did not assess combining two ACE inhibitors. - PMID:42077598

[D | hypothesis] Product labels (SmPCs) for ACE inhibitors and ARBs authorised in Poland mostly base renal dose adjustment on creatinine clearance; none uses GFR for dose adjustment, and recommendations are heterogeneous across products. Nephroprotective and antihypertensive maximum doses differed in some products, mainly lisinopril and benazepril. - PMID:42941287

[D | hypothesis] An open, non-comparative trial of fixed-dose losartan plus ramipril in Indian hypertensive diabetic patients reported blood pressure reduction, reduced albuminuria and high reported tolerability. - PMID:15636307
[D | hypothesis] In spontaneously hypertensive rats, losartan plus ramipril improved myocardial fibrosis and ultrastructure more than either drug alone. - PMID:16405840

[D | hypothesis] In Col4a3 knockout Alport mice, dapagliflozin added to ramipril preserved kidney function and histology better than ramipril alone and extended median survival. Dapagliflozin alone did not mitigate early GFR loss or albuminuria. - PMID:40499560

[D | hypothesis] A single case report suggests combined ACE and SGLT2 inhibition may haemodynamically attenuate GFR compensation, specifically after unilateral nephrectomy. The authors advise individualised management and close renal-function monitoring. - PMID:41737833

[D | hypothesis] In diabetic db/db mice, empagliflozin combined with ramipril prevented GFR increase (hyperfiltration). Metformin-ramipril-empagliflozin attenuated albuminuria and glomerulosclerosis. - PMID:32576600, PMID:36361612

[D | hypothesis] Low-level evidence shows that routine urinary and functional parameters may not reflect certain causes of kidney damage. In a small biopsy cohort and a case report, kidney biopsy identified tubulointerstitial and superimposed acute causes (Sjögren TIN, oxalate nephropathy) that routine tests did not reveal. - PMID:42931878, PMID:42942559

[D | hypothesis] In Col4a3-deficient mice with established nephropathy, late-onset ramipril monotherapy attenuated CKD and prolonged survival by about 2 weeks. Adding empagliflozin and finerenone extended survival further. - PMID:37428955

[D | emerging] In a small cohort of 45 patients with CKD G3b-4, aliskiren added to an ACEi or ARB reduced proteinuria with nearly stable potassium (4.9 to 5.0 mmol/L) and GFR. However, a creatinine rise above 30% was associated with UACR above 300 mg/g. The authors also note that earlier dual-blockade attempts in moderate CKD were terminated for hyperkalaemia and creatinine rise. - PMID:28449154

[D | hypothesis] In a rat ischaemia-reperfusion CKD model, combined losartan plus spironolactone showed the greatest benefit on CKD features, with fewer side effects at low dose. This is animal data on an ARB plus MRA combination, not an ACEi plus ARB. - PMID:31773183
[D | emerging] Genetic confirmation of Alport syndrome is described as facilitating RAS inhibitor use while avoiding unnecessary immunosuppressive therapy. - PMID:41555054

[D | hypothesis] In a preclinical randomized trial in Col4a3-deficient mice with established nephropathy, late-onset ramipril modestly prolonged survival. Treatment began after serum creatinine was elevated and fibrosis was present. Adding empagliflozin and finerenone extended survival further. - PMID:37428955

[D | hypothesis] For patients reaching ESRD or dialysis, one review reports lower cardiovascular event incidence in treated versus untreated ESRD patients with antihypertensives generally. It also notes that ARBs are not removed by dialysis, whereas ACE inhibitors are dialyzable. - PMID:42483492

Verified research findings (62)

items: [B | guideline supported] The ACC/AHA guideline uses persistent triglycerides ≥175 mg/dL as a risk-enhancing factor. It recommends repeat lipid measurement 4–12 weeks after statin initiation or dose change, then every 3–12 months as needed. The current triglyceride value of 79 mg/dL is below the risk-enhancing threshold. - PMID:30586774

[B | evidence supported] In a meta-analysis of 267 COL4A5 mutations in males, mutation type significantly predicted age at end-stage renal failure (ESRF). 5' glycine substitutions had the latest mean ESRF age at 30.1±7.2 years. Non-glycine or 3' glycine missense mutations had a mean ESRF age of 25.7±7.2 years. Large rearrangement, frameshift, nonsense and splice-donor mutations had a mean ESRF age of 19.8±5.7 years. - PMID:12105244

[B | evidence supported] Within families, the phenotype of an individual COL4A5 mutation was very consistent for deafness, lenticonus and timing of ESRF onset. Glycine substitutions were the most common mutation class. - PMID:12105244

[B | evidence supported] In males with X-linked Alport syndrome, COL4A5 mutation type significantly predicted age at end-stage renal failure. Glycine substitutions were associated with later ESRF than truncating mutations: 3' glycine-missense (grouped with non-glycine missense, in-frame indels and splice acceptor mutations) mean ESRF age 25.7±7.2 years; 5' glycine substitutions 30.1±7.2 years; large rearrangements, frameshift, nonsense and splice donor mutations 19.8±5.7 years. - PMID:12105244

[C | evidence supported] An acute decline in kidney function in someone with established CKD (AoCKD) is associated with increased mortality, accelerated CKD progression and higher cardiovascular risk. It is poorly defined in current KDIGO, ADQI and NICE frameworks. - PMID:33121629, PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] In CKD populations, creatinine-based definitions of acute deterioration have reduced prognostic accuracy. Cystatin C-based eGFR shows better discrimination for mortality and progression. - PMID:42954720

[C | evidence supported] Recommended initial evaluation of AKI has several parts: history and examination to classify the cause as prerenal, intrinsic renal or postrenal; laboratory work-up; medication adjustment; identification and reversal of the underlying cause; and specialist referral. - PMID:33121629

[C | evidence supported] NSAIDs are a recognised cause of acute and chronic kidney injury. Nephrotoxicity is increased by hypovolaemia, high-dose exposure, calcineurin inhibitors, RAAS inhibitors and diuretics. Early recognition can allow cessation of the NSAID and, in some cases, reversal of injury. - PMID:36947330

[C | evidence supported] Obstructive or infective postrenal causes such as pyonephrosis are potentially reversible causes of AKI. Guidelines strongly recommend urgent decompression, although the supporting data are observational. - PMID:42938174

[C | evidence supported] Point-of-care blood gas analysis may overestimate potassium and should be confirmed with a laboratory sample unless urgent treatment is required. When ECG changes are present, immediate cardiac protection is a priority. - PMID:42935704

[C | emerging] An acute decline in kidney function superimposed on established CKD (AoCKD) is a recognised but poorly defined clinical state. Reported incidence varies widely because criteria are inconsistent. The review links it to increased mortality even before formal KDIGO AKI thresholds are reached. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] In CKD populations, creatinine-based definitions of acute decline have reduced prognostic accuracy. Cystatin C-based eGFR showed superior discrimination for mortality and progression. - PMID:42954720

[C | evidence supported] In advanced CKD (stage 4), chlorthalidone produced reversible increases in serum creatinine more often than placebo. This illustrates that medication-related haemodynamic effects can contribute to creatinine changes. - PMID:34739197
[C | emerging] About one quarter of serum creatinine-defined AKI episodes in internal medicine wards were undocumented, especially those with lower maximal creatinine. - PMID:42703057

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews describe the typical CKD 'dyslipidemic profile' as including increased (not decreased) triglycerides. A large fall in triglycerides is therefore not the direction these sources associate with declining kidney function. - PMID:16973506, PMID:30519980

[C | evidence supported] Statins reduce triglyceride-rich remnant lipoproteins (IDL and VLDL-C) in CKD. If a statin or other lipid-lowering agent was started but not recorded, it could contribute to a triglyceride fall. - PMID:16973506

[C | evidence supported] Peritoneal dialysis is described as producing more severe dyslipidaemia than haemodialysis, through glucose absorption from dialysate stimulating hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Dialysis modality therefore affects expected lipid trajectories. - PMID:16973506

[C | emerging] In a pediatric XLAS cohort, male sex, splicing/deletion mutations and variants beyond exon 47 were associated with faster progression, and intronic mutations with better outcomes. The authors state that all findings are exploratory. No absolute eGFR decline rates for glycine missense variants are reported in the abstract. - PMID:42955328

[C | emerging] In a single-center adult Alport cohort (n=179), male sex and X-linked or autosomal recessive inheritance were associated with higher hazard of kidney failure with replacement therapy or CKD 3b. Eye and ear impairment carried a large but imprecise hazard ratio. Kidney cysts were associated with faster eGFR decline, but no absolute slope values are given. - PMID:41767691

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews describe the clinical course of Alport syndrome as highly variable. It is influenced by sex, inheritance mode, gene, mutation type and genetic modifiers. - PMID:39004457

[C | emerging] Acute decline in kidney function in people with established CKD (AoCKD) is not specifically addressed in major guideline frameworks. Definitions are heterogeneous, so there is no source-supported, guideline-specific evaluation algorithm for AKI on advanced CKD. - PMID:42954720

[C | evidence supported] KDIGO AKI criteria are time-bound: a creatinine rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or to at least 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. A baseline creatinine should be established for any suspected AKI episode. - PMID:28722925, PMID:33750089

[C | evidence supported] Newer KDIGO (2026) content, as reported in a study guide, suggests using serum cystatin C to identify AKI when creatinine is less accurate. An AoCKD review reports that cystatin C-based eGFR discriminates mortality and progression better than creatinine-based definitions in CKD populations. - PMID:28722925, PMID:42954720

[C | evidence supported] Identifying the cause of AKI is described as key to reversing it. Management is cause-specific plus supportive care for complications: volume overload, electrolyte disorders, uraemic complications and drug toxicity. The sources do not enumerate which specific tests to perform. - PMID:29114754, PMID:36336433

[C | evidence supported] Acute deterioration in CKD is associated with increased mortality, even below KDIGO-AKI thresholds. Recovery to dialysis independence is described as typical mainly for patients without premorbid CKD. These are associations, not causal estimates. - PMID:22617274, PMID:29114754, PMID:42954720
[C | emerging] Within families, the phenotype of a given COL4A5 mutation was very consistent for deafness, lenticonus and timing of ESRF onset. - PMID:12105244

[C | emerging] In an adult Alport cohort, risk factors for kidney failure or CKD 3b included male sex, X-linked or autosomal recessive inheritance, eye and ear impairment, higher baseline creatinine, proteinuria and earlier age at diagnosis. Kidney cysts were associated with faster eGFR decline. - PMID:41767691
[C | emerging] Clinical course and prognosis in Alport syndrome are highly variable, influenced by sex, inheritance mode, affected gene, mutation type and genetic modifiers. - PMID:39004457

[C | emerging] AoCKD lacks a harmonized definition and is underrepresented in major guideline frameworks (KDIGO, ADQI, NICE). Reported incidence varies widely because criteria are inconsistent. No guideline-endorsed AoCKD evaluation pathway is available in the provided sources. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] AoCKD is associated with increased mortality, accelerated CKD progression and higher cardiovascular risk. The review states that the increased mortality is seen even before the KDIGO-AKI threshold is reached. This supports recognizing acute deterioration early rather than attributing all decline to progression. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] In CKD populations, creatinine-based definitions of acute deterioration show reduced prognostic accuracy, whereas cystatin C-based eGFR shows superior discrimination for mortality and progression. A separate review notes that cystatin C refines functional assessment when creatinine is confounded by frailty, muscle mass or acute hemodynamic changes. - PMID:42511998, PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] Similar rises in serum creatinine can reflect very different mechanisms, which often coexist. These include reduced effective volume, congestion, tubular injury, infection, drug toxicity or interstitial nephritis, vascular thrombosis, or glomerular disease. Evaluation should therefore integrate serial assessment of perfusion, congestion, fluid balance, urine findings, drug exposures, infection, and vascular or intrinsic kidney disease rather than relying on creatinine alone. - PMID:42942510

[C | emerging] Urinary tubular injury and stress biomarkers (NGAL, KIM-1, [TIMP-2]·[IGFBP7]) may help separate functional filtration loss from tubular damage. However, they are described as adjuncts or a research horizon rather than an established basis for management. Point-of-care cystatin C systems remain investigational. - PMID:42783394, PMID:42942510

[C | emerging] In a pediatric XLAS cohort, male sex, deletion mutations and variants located beyond exon 47 were associated with faster renal decline. The abstract reports no numeric eGFR slopes and no glycine-specific or collagenous-domain-position analysis. The authors call all findings exploratory. - PMID:42955328

[C | emerging] In an adult Chinese Alport cohort (n=179), male sex and X-linked or autosomal recessive inheritance were associated with higher hazard of kidney failure with replacement therapy or CKD G3b. Baseline creatinine, proteinuria and eye/ear impairment were also associated. Kidney cysts were associated with about a 2-fold faster eGFR slope. Absolute slope values by genotype were not reported in the abstract. - PMID:41767691

[C | evidence supported] Reviews state that the clinical course of Alport syndrome is highly variable. It is influenced by sex, inheritance mode, affected gene, mutation type and genetic modifiers, and genotype-phenotype correlations differ between X-linked and autosomal dominant disease. - PMID:39004457, PMID:39840589

[C | emerging] In males with X-linked Alport syndrome, the 2002 meta-analysis assigned 3' glycine missense mutations to an intermediate group (mean ESRF age 25.7±7.2 y) and 5' glycine substitutions to a later-onset group (30.1±7.2 y). The abstract does not define the exon or residue boundary between 5' and 3'. - PMID:12105244

[C | emerging] A later study stratified COL4A5 glycine substitutions by exon location (exons 1–20 vs 21 to carboxyl terminus) and found exon location had no effect. This argues against a strong prognostic 5'/3' positional split, although its boundary may differ from the 2002 definition. - PMID:35177655

[C | emerging] Among COL4A5 glycine substitutions in males, a highly destabilising replacement residue was associated with a median age at kidney failure about 7 years earlier. Glu is listed among the highly destabilising residues, though that list appears in the COL4A3/COL4A4 analysis. - PMID:35177655

[C | emerging] Glycine substitutions adjacent to a non-collagenous region (interruption or terminus) were associated with kidney failure delayed by about 19 years. The sources do not state whether Gly1048 is adjacent to such a region. - PMID:35177655

[C | emerging] Older single-country data reported a mean ESRD age of 35.8 years for collagenous-domain glycine substitutions. The same author concluded that the lack of distinct genotype-phenotype correlations limits the prognostic usefulness of COL4A5 mutation type. - PMID:19728970
[C | emerging] The 2002 meta-analysis found that the phenotype of an individual COL4A5 mutation is very consistent within a family, including timing of ESRF onset. - PMID:12105244

[C | emerging] A 2026 critical review reports that acute deterioration on established CKD (AoCKD) is underrepresented in current KDIGO, ADQI and NICE guideline frameworks. This suggests, second-hand, that current KDIGO AKI guidance may not contain a dedicated AoCKD evaluation pathway. The primary guideline text was not available to verify this. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] Definitions of acute deterioration in CKD are heterogeneous (AoCKD, AKI-on-CKD, acute pre-existing kidney dysfunction, cROCK-based). Reported incidence varies widely because criteria are inconsistent. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] In CKD populations, creatinine-based acute decline definitions show reduced prognostic accuracy. Cystatin C-based eGFR is reported to discriminate better for mortality and progression, and the review proposes incorporating cystatin C-based markers into AoCKD definitions. - PMID:42954720

[C | emerging] For contrast-associated AKI specifically, an audit describes international guideline (KDIGO/ESUR) recommendations: risk assessment, appropriate hydration, medication review and patient counselling. This is second-hand and limited to contrast exposure; it is not a general AoCKD evaluation framework. - PMID:42787955

[C | emerging] A KDIGO Controversies Conference report highlights the need for refined AKI definitions in heart failure. It notes that small kidney function declines after guideline-directed HF therapy are often hemodynamic and not associated with poor outcomes, showing that context-specific interpretation of creatinine changes in CKD is an acknowledged gap. - PMID:41791738, PMID:41793402

[C | emerging] In a retrospective two-centre Alport syndrome cohort of mixed inheritance modes, rapid eGFR decline was defined as a loss of more than 6 mL/min/1.73m2 per year, and about a quarter of patients met this definition. Albuminuria was independently associated with yearly eGFR loss. - PMID:42415835
[C | emerging] In adult Alport patients with significant proteinuria on stable RASi, the chronic eGFR slope before SGLT2i was about -3.48 mL/min/1.73m2 per year. - PMID:42006198

[C | emerging] The most severe Alport forms, which lack the collagen α3α4α5(IV) network, are described as progressing to kidney failure by about age 30. This implies faster progression in severe genotypes, but no eGFR slope is given. - PMID:41183732

[C | emerging] Genotype-phenotype correlations: missense, mainly Gly, substitutions are generally associated with later-onset kidney failure than truncating or large rearrangement variants. Substitution of Gly by more disruptive residues (including Glu) is listed as a determinant of greater severity in XLAS males. - PMID:35602506
[C | emerging] Male sex and X-linked or autosomal recessive inheritance were associated with higher risk of kidney failure or CKD G3b in an adult Alport cohort. - PMID:41767691

[C | emerging] Proteinuria and eGFR decline in Alport syndrome are expected to follow nonlinear trajectories. Interpretation should account for genotype, sex, age, baseline eGFR and disease duration, which limits linear extrapolation of short-interval slopes. - PMID:42949772

[D | hypothesis] Similar rises in serum creatinine can arise from heterogeneous, often coexisting mechanisms. These include reduced effective arterial volume, volume expansion, tubular stress or injury, infection or sepsis, drug toxicity or acute interstitial nephritis, vascular thrombosis, or the underlying glomerular disease. Serial multimodal assessment is advised rather than reliance on creatinine alone. - PMID:42942510

[D | emerging] In a 25-week non-randomised cohort of adults with MASLD, triglycerides fell significantly with both saroglitazar and dapagliflozin. This illustrates that some metabolic agents can lower triglycerides substantially. - PMID:42967591

[D | hypothesis] In dialysis-dependent CKD, malnutrition-inflammation is treated as a confounder of the relationship between lipid levels (total cholesterol) and mortality. Whether this patient's lower triglycerides reflect nutritional or inflammatory status is only a hypothesis based on that context. - PMID:16973506

[D | emerging] Imaging pathways and early kidney-damage biomarkers for AoCKD are described as needing harmonisation, so the sources give no evidence-based imaging protocol. - PMID:22617274, PMID:42954720

[D | hypothesis] In a pediatric X-linked Alport cohort, male sex, deletion mutations and mutations beyond exon 47 suggested faster renal decline; the authors state these findings are exploratory. - PMID:42955328

[D | hypothesis] Admission cystatin C, together with CKD and diuretic use, was among the predictors in a model of in-hospital AKI in elderly heart failure patients. This supports cystatin C as a risk-stratification marker in a different population. - PMID:42829622

[D | hypothesis] Indirect evidence from COL4A3/COL4A4 (not COL4A5) shows glycine substitutions associated with worse kidney outcomes. This cannot be directly extrapolated to hemizygous COL4A5 males. - PMID:40806767

[D | hypothesis] The AoCKD review calls for structured imaging pathways and early biomarkers. This implies these elements (e.g., imaging for obstruction) are not yet harmonised within guideline frameworks, but no specific imaging recommendation from KDIGO is quoted in the sources. - PMID:42954720

[E | hypothesis] The provided sources do not specify an imaging protocol (e.g., kidney ultrasound or Doppler) for evaluating AoCKD. The AoCKD review only states that structured imaging pathways are urgently needed. - PMID:42954720

[C | evidence supported] In males with a pathogenic COL4A5 variant, all collagen IV α3α4α5 heterotrimers are affected. This is the genetic rationale for COL4A5 as the disease-driving target in hemizygous males. - PMID:35675912

[D | hypothesis] Glycine substitutions at position 1 of the collagen repeat in COL4A3-COL4A5 are associated with hematuria in population data. Penetrance varies, and many COL4A5 variants carry features that may mitigate their effect. - PMID:34400539

[D | hypothesis] Proposed therapeutic strategies directed at the collagen IV defect itself include reconstituting the α3α4α5(IV) network in the GBM and chaperone therapy. The review adds that the dominant mechanisms differ across the disease course. - PMID:40938675

[D | hypothesis] Genetic-level approaches are described as advancing toward precision medicine for Alport syndrome: exon skipping, gene editing and nonsense readthrough (ELX-02). RAAS blockade remains foundational but does not target the molecular defect. - PMID:41243004
[D | hypothesis] In HeLa and 293T cells, anticodon-edited tRNAs restored full-length translation across four COL4A5 nonsense variants. - PMID:41417821

[D | hypothesis] In female Col4a5 heterozygous mice, Minnelide reduced proteinuria, upregulated renal Col4a5 and suppressed ER stress. The parent compound triptolide is limited by toxicity. - PMID:41737559
[D | hypothesis] Downstream modulation, such as STAT3 inhibition, ameliorated renal dysfunction in a Col4a5 mutant mouse model. - PMID:28992339

[C | evidence supported] Clinical evidence for standard RAAS blockade is that it slows but does not stop progression. A pediatric Indian cohort found no significant ACEI effect on proteinuria or CKD. - PMID:27190345, PMID:42955332

[C | evidence supported] Safety in family planning and transplantation: affected relatives should be identified, treated and discouraged from kidney donation, and cascade testing of first-degree relatives is advocated. - PMID:34930753, PMID:35675912
[D | hypothesis] A single family report raises the possibility that COL4A5 variants contribute to cerebrovascular fragility. - PMID:42881817

[D | hypothesis] Co-occurrence of ADPKD (PKD1) and Alport syndrome (COL4A5) is documented only in rare case reports. In a small literature review of such dual cases, prognosis was poor, with most progressing to kidney failure. This is association and case-level description, not evidence that PKD1 drives or modifies Alport disease, and not evidence for PKD1 modulation. - PMID:41557100, PMID:41765374

[D | emerging] Kidney cysts/PKD are described as an emerging manifestation of COL4A3-A5 (collagen IV) disease itself. Alport syndrome can be misdiagnosed as ADPKD. Cysts in a COL4A5 patient therefore do not by themselves imply PKD1 involvement. - PMID:38790225, PMID:40683378

[D | hypothesis] In Pkd1-mutant mouse and cell models, several interventions slowed cyst growth and/or fibrosis: Runx1 inhibition, KCa3.1 blockade (senicapoc), inflammasome inhibition (MCC950), recombinant Klotho and pirfenidone. These act on pathways downstream of Pkd1 loss, not on PKD1 itself. – was studied in Alport/COL4A5 models or in humans, and no safety data are reported. - PMID:40909512, PMID:41122971, PMID:41231953, PMID:42314074, PMID:42640700

[D | hypothesis] ADPKD fibrosis involves inflammatory and TGF-beta/SMAD signalling with expansion of extracellular matrix, including collagen IV. This suggests only a conceptual overlap of fibrotic pathways with collagen IV disease. The sources do not show that targeting PKD1-related pathways benefits Alport syndrome. - PMID:31399962

[C | evidence supported] VUS interpretation in hereditary kidney disease benefits from family co-segregation studies. Apparent non-segregation in a mother with a compatible phenotype may reflect low-level mosaicism detectable only by high-sensitivity sequencing. - PMID:38418364, PMID:41765374, PMID:41901018

[C | emerging] In a single-centre genetic-testing cohort of suspected inherited kidney disease, kidney survival differed by genetic subgroup. PKD2-variant carriers had more favourable outcomes, while COL4A5-associated Alport syndrome progressed rapidly. This compares different diseases and does not show that modulating PKD2 alters Alport progression. - PMID:42389199

[D | hypothesis] Loss-of-function of PKD2 is an established cause of ADPKD. Any strategy that reduces polycystin-2 function therefore carries a theoretical risk of reproducing ADPKD-like cystic pathology. This is an inference from disease genetics; no source tested PKD2 inhibition in Alport syndrome. - PMID:42193072

[D | hypothesis] In animal and cell models, polycystins have endothelial protective roles. Zebrafish screening identified PKD1 and PKD2 as anti-apoptotic endothelial factors. In mice, endothelial-specific loss of PKD1, but not PKD2, increased atherosclerosis. This suggests possible vascular off-target effects of polycystin modulation; PKD2-specific vascular risk is uncertain. - PMID:42573181

[E | hypothesis] The PKD-pathway therapy discussed in the sources (tolvaptan) is approved for ADPKD only. Its use is limited by side effects and cost. No source evaluates it, or other polycystin-pathway agents, in Alport syndrome. - PMID:42193072

[C | emerging] In a male with a pathogenic COL4A5 variant, all collagen IV α3α4α5 heterotrimers are affected, and an additional COL4A3 or COL4A4 variant may not worsen disease. In women with a COL4A5 variant, an added COL4A3/COL4A4 variant raises the affected heterotrimer fraction from about 50% to 75% and is linked to more proteinuria. Together this suggests that in hemizygous males the α5 defect dominates, and changing α4 alone is unlikely to restore the heterotrimer. - PMID:35675912

MXR-RES-002 Hb above 125 g/L in ESA-treated haemodialysis patients - possible mortality signal - Haemoglobin, whole blood gt 125 g/L (Adults on maintenance haemodialysis for at least 3 months receiving ESA (darbepoetin) therapy); grade C
MXR-RES-003 Rapid eGFR decline flag in Alport syndrome - Annual eGFR loss (eGFR slope, absolute decline) gt 6 mL/min/1.73m2 per year (patients with Alport syndrome); grade C

MXR-RES-004 Admission anemia flag in critically ill non-trauma ED patients - Hemoglobin lt 12 g/dL (Adult critically ill non-trauma patients at emergency department/resuscitation room admission only (not outpatient CKD)); grade D
MXR-RES-005 Dietary sodium above KDIGO 2024 limit in CKD - Estimated dietary sodium record gt 2 g/day (Adults with CKD (KDIGO 2024 lifestyle recommendation as summarized)); grade C
MXR-RES-006 High-risk (CKD) blood pressure threshold - systolic - Systolic blood pressure ge 130 mm[Hg] (adults with chronic kidney disease (ACC/AHA high-risk category)); grade C
MXR-RES-007 High-risk (CKD) blood pressure threshold - diastolic - Diastolic blood pressure ge 80 mm[Hg] (adults with chronic kidney disease (ACC/AHA high-risk category)); grade C

MXR-RES-008 Hb above 125 g/L in ESA-treated haemodialysis adult - flag for target review - Haemoglobin, whole blood gt 125 g/L (Adults on maintenance haemodialysis for at least 3 months receiving ESA (darbepoetin) therapy); grade C
MXR-RES-009 Advanced CKD ACEi/ARB evidence applicability - Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI 2021, creatinine) lt 30 mL/min/1.73m2 (adults with CKD and eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2); grade B

MXR-RES-010 Advanced CKD ACEi/ARB evidence applicability flag - Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI 2021, creatinine) lt 30 mL/min/1.73m2 (Adults with non-dialysis CKD and eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 being considered for ACEi/ARB); grade B
MXR-RES-011 ESA initiation threshold - CKD on dialysis (label) - Haemoglobin, whole blood lt 10 g/dL (adults with CKD on dialysis); grade D
MXR-RES-012 ESA consideration threshold - CKD not on dialysis (label) - Haemoglobin, whole blood lt 10 g/dL (adults with CKD not on dialysis); grade D
MXR-RES-013 Hb above 11 g/dL safety flag in ESA-treated CKD - Haemoglobin, whole blood gt 11 g/dL (adults with CKD receiving an ESA); grade D
MXR-RES-014 PIVOTAL reactive IV iron trigger: ferritin - Ferritin, serum lt 200 ug/L (Adults on maintenance haemodialysis (trial protocol, low-dose reactive arm)); grade B
MXR-RES-015 PIVOTAL reactive IV iron trigger: TSAT - Transferrin saturation lt 20 % (Adults on maintenance haemodialysis (trial protocol, low-dose reactive arm)); grade B
MXR-RES-016 PIVOTAL proactive IV iron withholding threshold: ferritin - Ferritin, serum gt 700 ug/L (Adults on maintenance haemodialysis receiving proactive IV iron (trial protocol)); grade B
MXR-RES-017 PIVOTAL proactive IV iron withholding threshold: TSAT - Transferrin saturation ge 40 % (Adults on maintenance haemodialysis receiving proactive IV iron (trial protocol)); grade B

MXR-RES-018 Advanced CKD referral for KRT planning - Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI creatinine) lt 20 mL/min/1.73m2 (Adults with advanced CKD (practice in a UK tertiary advanced kidney care service)); grade C

MXR-RES-019 Dapagliflozin initiation not recommended at low eGFR - Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI 2021, creatinine) lt 25 mL/min/1.73m2 (Adults with renal impairment being considered for dapagliflozin for an indication other than glycaemic control); grade D
MXR-RES-020 Sparsentan on-treatment aminotransferase elevation >3x ULN - Alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase, serum gt 3 x ULN (Patients receiving sparsentan (FILSPARI)); grade D
MXR-RES-021 Sparsentan baseline aminotransferase >3x ULN - Alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase, serum gt 3 x ULN (Patients being considered for sparsentan initiation); grade D

MXR-RES-022 Finerenone evidence outside trial eGFR range - Estimated GFR (CKD-EPI 2021, creatinine) lt 25 mL/min/1.73m2 (Adults with non-diabetic proteinuric CKD being considered for finerenone); grade C
